articles.title: Mães solo celebram fim da escala 6x1: 'Estava vendo a vida dos meus filhos passar' | G1
articles.standfirst: Trabalhadoras sem rede de apoio relatam dificuldades que a jornada 6x1 impunha na convivência com os filhos e como isso pode mudar daqui para a frente.
articles.summary: Trabalhadoras sem rede de apoio relatam dificuldades que a jornada 6x1 impunha na convivência com os filhos e como isso pode mudar daqui para a frente.
articles.body:
Às 5h, Luciana de Almeida, de 36 anos, já está de pé para começar a organizar o dia. Arruma as duas filhas caçulas, serve o café da manhã e segue para deixá-las na escola, em Realengo, no Rio de Janeiro.

Filhas em sala de aula, a operadora de caixa embarca no transporte público por 1h30 para chegar ao supermercado onde trabalha na escala 6x1, em Campo Grande, a cerca de 20 quilômetros.

Almoço às 15h, saída registrada no ponto às 17h50 e, duas horas depois, perto das 20h, Luciana está de volta em casa, liberando o filho mais velho de 15 anos do cuidado com as irmãs, de 4 anos e 1 ano e 8 meses.

No único dia de folga que tem na semana, sobra pouco para o descanso diante das tarefas domésticas. Muitas vezes, ainda faz faxinas para conseguir uma renda extra para sustentar a família como mãe solo, conta.

"Estou com o corpo e, principalmente, com a mente muito cansados", diz Luciana, que trabalha na escala 6x1 no comércio desde os 18 anos. "No dia depois da folga, eu continuo trabalhando cansada."

Não é de se estranhar que, nos últimos meses, a carioca acompanhou atenta às discussões da PEC que encerrou essa modalidade de trabalho.

Segundo o Ministério do Trabalho, no final de 2025, a escala 6x1 era a realidade de 14,8 milhões de trabalhadores no Brasil , que representam pouco mais de um terço da mão de obra formal.

A implementação ocorrerá em duas fases. A primeira terá início 60 dias após a promulgação do texto, garantindo o fim da escala 6x1 e reduzindo a jornada de trabalho de 44 para 42 horas semanais. Depois de 14 meses, a carga horária será reduzida de 42 para 40 horas semanais.

Após a aprovação no Senado , o texto ainda precisará ser promulgado em sessão solene pelas Mesas Diretoras da Câmara e do Senado para, enfim, ser publicado e passar a integrar a Constituição.

Assim, passados todos esses prazos, a carioca vai viver agora a primeira experiência em sua vida com duas folgas na semanas.

"Vai mudar muita coisa", diz. "Vou conseguir descansar, resolver coisas da minha vida, até fazer um extra se conseguir."

Outro ponto de virada na vida de Luciana será acompanhar mais a vida dos filhos que, segundo ela, está "passando" sem que ela esteja presente.

Foi nas férias desse ano, em uma rotina em casa, que ela teve essa reflexão: "Estou vendo a vida dos meus filhos passar, não consigo ir em festa de dia das mães, junina, nada", diz.

"Preciso ter tempo com minhas filhas, ter algum lazer ou mesmo ficar em casa descansando", relata.

A carioca diz não saber como será a readaptação na empresa onde trabalha e que vive uma expectativa pela eleição presidencial. Isso porque diz não saber o que aconteceria com uma eventual eleição de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para presidente .

Flávio, que é senador, se posicionara, na terça-feira, pela primeira vez, a favor do fim da escala 6x1 — e votou pela aprovação.

Até então, ele dizia que a proposta era "oportunista", por ir a votação às vésperas das eleições.

A proposta foi apresentada por parlamentares da esquerda e uma das maiores bandeiras da campanha de reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

"A maioria dos trabalhadores brasileiros quer o fim da 6x1, então eu vou votar a favor do fim da 6x1", disse Flávio.

O senador também segue defendendo uma "jornada flexível", na qual, segundo ele, empregador e empregado chegariam a um consenso sobre as condições de trabalho.

Antes da votação, o líder do PL na Câmara dos Deputados, Sóstenes Cavalcante disse que Flávio vai insistir, depois das eleições, na votação da chamada "PEC das horas".

A proposta, de autoria de Rogerio Marinho (PL-RN), prevê que o trabalhador escolha entre seguir o regime de trabalho tradicional previsto pela CLT, ou um regime flexível baseado em horas trabalhadas.

Setor de serviços e comércio terão que passar por maiores adaptações diante do fim da escala 6x1 — Foto: Dado Galdieri/Bloomberg via Getty Images/BBC

Em São Paulo, a gerente comercial Fabiane da Conceição, 50 anos, também comemorou a aprovação do fim da escala 6x1.

Foram 20 anos de sua vida se dedicando ao trabalho com apenas uma folga na semana. Há 30 dias, a paulistana assumiu um novo emprego na escala 5x2, mas diz que guarda na memória as dificuldades que enfrentou, especialmente na relação com os dois filhos que criou sozinha.

"Sinto hoje que perdi a maior parte das coisas que enxergo importante na criação dos filhos. Não os vi aprender a andar, não os levei ao primeiro dia da escola", conta Fabiane, emocionada.

"Eu não posso me arrepender porque era o que dava nosso sustento, mas não deixo de sentir a dor. Me sinto aliviada quando penso em pessoas mais jovens e outras mulheres que vão viver uma situação que não às leve à exaustão física e mental e à exclusão materna."

Fabiane passou por lojas no comércio e serviços na indústria alimentícia, automotiva e petrolífera. Mãe de dois filhos e vítima de violência doméstica por parte do ex-marido, ela não tinha uma rede de apoio para auxiliá-la.

"Lembro que, 30 anos atrás, eu ganhava R$ 400 reais e pagava R$ 180 para alguém pegar meus filhos na escola e ficar com eles até o momento que eu chegava em casa, às 20h", lembra. Ela encarava 2 horas no transporte entre Sapopemba, onde morava, na Zona Leste da capital paulista, e a Barra Funda, onde trabalhava, na Zona Oeste.

"Sempre tive total noção da qualidade de vida que eu não tinha. Mas o fator financeiro me exigia, era isso ou não tinha dinheiro em casa. Deixou de ser escolha para mim muito cedo", completa.

A paulistana diz que a relação com os filhos acabou ficando marcada por mágoas deixadas por sua ausência em casa. "Me dói muito saber que o tempo que eu tinha era pouco para eles. Que sentiam minha falta", diz.

"Pela primeira vez, mães como eu poderiam ter dia de lazer, organizar a vida, ficar em casa e poder descansar."

Luciana vive expectativa por ter duas folgas na semana para conviver mais com três filhos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal via BBC

articles.title: Plenário do Senado deve votar nesta quinta PEC da Segurança Pública | G1
articles.standfirst: Tema é considerado prioritário para governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que pretende, após aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.
articles.summary: Tema é considerado prioritário para governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que pretende, após aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.
articles.body:
O plenário do Senado Federal deve votar nesta quinta-feira (15) a proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública. O tema é considerado prioritário para o governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que pretende, após a aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.

🔎 Para ser aprovada, uma PEC precisa ter ao menos três quintos dos votos favoráveis nas duas votações. Ou seja, precisa contar com o apoio de 49 senadores.

O parecer do senador Rogério Carvalho (PT-SE) rejeitou as mudanças propostas e manteve o texto aprovado pela Câmara dos Deputados . A estratégia é agilizar a aprovação final para concluir a votação antes do segundo turno das eleições.

Na noite desta quarta, o plenário do Senado aprovou um calendário especial para quebrar o interstício – período previsto no regimento interno do Senado que prevê cinco sessões de debate antes da votação da proposta em primeiro turno, mais cinco dias úteis e três outras sessões de debate para a votação do segundo turno.

Com isso, os senadores não precisarão cumprir cinco sessões de discussão antes de analisar a proposta e poderão votar o texto em dois turnos, sem intervalo entre as votações.

A proposta estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (SUSP), cujo objetivo é integrar o combate ao crime organizado entre os entes.

De acordo com o texto, União, Estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, organização das polícias e guardas municipais e do sistema socioeducativo.

Outro ponto central da PEC da Segurança Pública é sobre o combate a crimes violentos e facções criminosas.

Entre as medidas estão a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial.

Também fica proibida ou restringida a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária.

A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvido com as atividades criminosas. As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

criação de polícias municipais para o policiamento ostensivo e comunitário;

ampliação da atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) para o policiamento de hidrovias e ferrovias, além de apoiar outras forças de segurança, quando requisitada pelo governador;

manter a Polícia Federal e PRF sob competência privativa da União, assim como as normas para atividades de inteligência.

Plenário do Senado Federal — Foto: Carlos Moura/Agência Senado

O PL e os partidos de oposição ao governo Lula (PT) no Senado apresentaram uma emenda para incluir a redução da maioridade penal na PEC da Segurança Pública.

A emenda proposta pela oposição incluiria duas alterações na proposta, reduzindo a maioridade penal:

para 16 anos para a maior parte dos crimes; e

para 14 anos para crimes hediondos, tortura, tráfico de drogas, terrorismo, organização criminosa, associação criminosa e outros.

A emenda foi apresentada pelo senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), coordenador da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à Presidência. Flávio anunciou a medida em suas redes sociais e também assina a emenda.

Segundo Marinho, é preciso punir os adolescentes para que eles não sejam cooptados pelo crime organizado. A redução da maioridade é uma defesa do campo político bolsonarista.

Já há uma PEC específica sobre isso sendo analisada no Congresso Nacional. Atualmente, a Câmara tem uma comissão específica para analisar o tema. Ainda no meio do ano, deputados da oposição afirmaram que era necessário discutir o tema com seriedade e responsabilidade.

A oposição no Senado, no entanto, quer incluir o tema na PEC do governo, que não tem ligação direta com o tema.

O tema é considerado prioritário para o governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) que pretende, após a aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.

A ideia é que a pasta seja permanente e não corra o risco de ser extinta por um decreto presidencial, dando mais garantia à população de que uma política nacional de segurança pública se manterá.

Após a conclusão da aprovação da PEC da Segurança na Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ), o presidente Lula ligou para o senador Otto Alencar (PSD-BA) , que preside o colegiado, para agradecer pela aprovação.

Segundo apurou o g1, o principal articulador para a votação acontecer no Senado foi o líder do MDB no Senado, Eduardo Braga (AM), que esteve trabalhando nos bastidores para conseguir assinaturas para a aprovação de um calendário especial para acelerar a tramitação da matéria.

articles.title: Fim da escala 6x1: veja como votaram os senadores do Piauí | G1
articles.standfirst: O texto garante dois dias de folga por semana ao trabalhador, sem diminuição do salário, e foi aprovado em dois turnos de votação.
articles.summary: O texto garante dois dias de folga por semana ao trabalhador, sem diminuição do salário, e foi aprovado em dois turnos de votação.
articles.body:
O Senado aprovou a Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que acaba com a escala 6x1 , na quarta-feira (14). No segundo turno da votação, os três senadores do Piauí, Ciro Nogueira (Progressistas), Jussara Lima (PSD) e Marcelo Castro (MDB) votaram a favor da redução da carga horária dos trabalhadores.

O texto garante dois dias de folga por semana ao trabalhador, sem diminuição do salário , e foi aprovado em dois turnos de votação. Nos dois turnos, o texto teve 75 votos a favor e um contra. O texto garante dois dias de folga por semana ao trabalhador, sem diminuição do salário, e foi aprovado em dois turnos de votação.

Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) do fim da jornada 6x1

A PEC do fim da jornada 6x1 altera a Constituição para diminuir as horas de trabalho semanais de 44 para 40 horas. Também estabelece que é necessário garantir dois dias de folga remunerada, um deles preferencialmente aos domingos.

articles.title: Regra de transição e dois dias de folga: entenda como ficou a proposta que acaba com a escala 6x1 | G1
articles.standfirst: Texto ainda precisa ser promulgado. Previsão é que isso ocorra na semana que vem.
articles.summary: Texto ainda precisa ser promulgado. Previsão é que isso ocorra na semana que vem.
articles.body:
Plenário do Senado Federal — Foto: Jonas Pereira/Agência Senado

O Senado aprovou nesta quarta-feira (14) a Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que acaba com a escala 6x1 e garante dois dias de folga por semana para o trabalhador sem diminuição do salário.

O texto ainda precisa ser promulgado para entrar em vigor. A previsão é que isso ocorra na semana que vem.

Mas, para que os trabalhadores brasileiros cheguem à nova jornada, haverá ainda uma transição.

O período para a adaptação das empresas terá início logo depois da promulgação:

em dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 42 horas, com dois dias de repouso semanal remunerado;

em um ano após esses dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 40 horas.

🎯Depois de 14 meses da promulgação, a jornada máxima será reduzida em definitivo sem redução de salário.

Segundo as novas regras, o trabalhador terá direito a dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana, em vez da possibilidade atual de trabalhar seis dias e ter apenas um dia de folga.

A redução da jornada não acaba com as horas extras nem com mecanismos de compensação, como o banco de horas.

Esses instrumentos ainda poderão ser utilizados, desde que respeitem os novos limites e as regras previstas na legislação e nos acordos ou convenções coletivas.

Durante a transição, a negociação coletiva também poderá estabelecer formas de distribuição das horas trabalhadas para facilitar a adaptação das empresas.

Algumas categorias terão regras específicas. Atividades contínuas e essenciais, como saúde, segurança, transporte e limpeza urbana, poderão adotar formas diferentes de organização da jornada por meio de acordos ou convenções coletivas.

Também há regras específicas para trabalhadores com diploma de curso superior que recebam mais de 2,5 vezes o teto da Previdência Social, ou seja, quem ganhe mais de R$ 21.188 por mês.

Para esses profissionais, os limites gerais de jornada e as regras de controle de horário terão tratamento diferenciado, mas permanece o direito a dois dias de descanso por semana.

No caso dos trabalhadores terceirizados que prestam serviços à administração pública, a redução da jornada dependerá da assinatura de um termo aditivo aos contratos.

Os órgãos públicos terão até um ano para fazer essa alteração. Se não houver acordo nesse prazo, a redução passará a valer automaticamente.

Os microempreendedores individuais (MEIs), microempresas e empresas de pequeno porte também são citados no texto. A PEC prevê a aprovação de lei complementar com regras específicas para a transição, desde que sejam preservados os níveis de emprego nesses segmentos.

articles.title: Após cobrar debate, oposição só participa da última de cinco sessões de discussão da PEC do fim da escala 6x1 | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta foi aprovada por ampla maioria no Senado nesta quarta-feira (14). Texto precisa ser promulgado pelo Congresso Nacional antes de passar a valer.
articles.summary: Proposta foi aprovada por ampla maioria no Senado nesta quarta-feira (14). Texto precisa ser promulgado pelo Congresso Nacional antes de passar a valer.
articles.body:
Senadores de oposição ao governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) só participaram da última das cinco sessões de discussão da PEC que acaba com a escala 6x1. A proposta foi aprovada pelo Senado nesta quarta-feira (14).

A PEC garante dois dias de folga por semana para o trabalhador sem diminuição do salário e foi aprovada por 75 votos favoráveis contra 1, apenas do senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS). Agora, o texto espera por promulgação do Congresso Nacional antes de passar a valer.

Desde que a proposta chegou ao Senado , no final de maio deste ano, a oposição defendia que era preciso discutir de forma aprofundada a reforma. No entanto, a oposição não se manifestou nas quatro primeiras sessões destinadas ao debate do texto.

🔎 De acordo com o regimento interno do Senado, uma PEC precisa passar por cinco sessões de discussão em plenário antes de ser votada em primeiro turno. Para ser aprovada, uma PEC precisa ter ao menos três quintos dos votos favoráveis nas duas votações. Ou seja, precisa contar com o apoio de 49 senadores.

"Durante todo esse processo, nós nos posicionamos querendo uma discussão. Qual discussão? Aquela que inseriria a proposta do senador Rogério Marinho, para que a gente pudesse trazer, como se faz aqui em audiências públicas, todos os setores da economia, para que cada um possa saber o impacto na sua vida", afirmou o líder do PL no Senado, Carlos Portinho (RJ), nesta quarta.

Nas quatro primeiras sessões, que serviram apenas para debater o texto, nenhum senador da oposição se manifestou.

Apenas um parlamentar, Oriovisto Guimarães (PR), de um partido independente dentro do Senado, PSDB, fez ressalvas à proposta. O paranaense era contra o período de transição da PEC, que prevê 14 meses para aplicação das novas regras.

Nesta quarta, quatro senadores do PL e três do Republicanos decidiram discursar na tribuna.

Partidos da oposição – PL, PP, Republicanos, Novo e Avante – se posicionaram inicialmente contra o fim da escala 6x1.

Eles defendem uma PEC alternativa de pagamento por horas, modelo em que o trabalhador só receberia pela hora trabalhada e poderia ter seu salário diminuído de forma proporcional.

Essa proposta alternativa foi apresentada pelo coordenador da campanha do candidato do PL à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro, o senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN).

Colegas parlamentares comemoram enquanto o presidente do Senado Federal, Davi Alcolumbre, anuncia o resultado da votação a favor de uma emenda constitucional que reduz a jornada de trabalho no Brasil de seis para cinco dias, em Brasília, Brasil, 14 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Adriano Machado

Com o tema ganhando tração na campanha eleitoral e com cobranças públicas de Lula, na terça (13), Flávio afirmou que se posicionaria “conforme a vontade da maioria do povo”.

Nesta quarta, Flávio votou, de forma virtual, a favor da medida , mas sem participar da sessão. Ele cumpriu agenda de campanha em Porto Alegre.

O PL liberou a bancada para cada senador votar como desejava enquanto falam em mudanças depois das eleições. Mas o líder do PL na Câmara dos Deputados, Sóstenes Cavalcante (RJ), afirmou nesta quarta que Flávio Bolsonaro vai insistir na PEC das horas trabalhadas depois das eleições.

Nessa nova modalidade, segundo o deputado, não haveria salário-mínimo ou um mínimo de horas que o trabalhador teria direito a trabalhar semanalmente. Na proposta de hora trabalhada, hora paga, haveria espaço para diminuição do salário.

Ao ser questionado sobre direitos como 13º e férias remuneradas, Sóstenes disse que a proposta do PL não prevê esses direitos. "A PEC não é CLT, você tem que mudar o chip", disse o deputado.

Carlos Portinho (RJ) também disse que a regra pode ser alterada para comportar uma compensação para as empresas.

"Se isso aqui trazer danos para a economia, o próximo governo vai ter de encontrar as soluções. A gente já está pensando nisso. Se o empresário, quem empreende, se ele tiver prejuízo, começar a fechar negócio, começar a diminuir e não ter margem, acabar quebrando, a gente vai ter que encontrar solução para o problema que o Lula vai criar, para o outro lado da mesa. Já encontramos soluções, como foi no governo passado, com a desoneração", declarou.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula: Tarcísio e Alckmin reforçam campanhas | G1
articles.standfirst: Governador reeleito de São Paulo prometeu “mergulhar de cabeça” na campanha de Flávio no segundo turno; vice-presidente intensifica compromissos em estados estratégicos para a campanha petista.
articles.summary: Tarcísio de Freitas e Geraldo Alckmin intensificam agendas em estados estratégicos para atrair eleitores e fortalecer as campanhas de Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula no segundo turno.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos); Geraldo Alckmin (PSB) e Lula (PT) — Foto: Roberto Sungi/Ato Press/Estadão Conteúdo e Ricardo Stuckert/PR

Os candidatos à presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT), têm contado com dois aliados próximos nesta reta final de campanha para atrair votos: o governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), e o vice-presidente, Geraldo Alckmin (PSB).

Tarcísio acompanhará Flávio em ao menos três viagens para capitais. Nesta quarta (14), estiveram juntos em Porto Alegre . No fim de semana, a previsão é de que viajem para Vitória e Salvador. Integrantes da campanha avaliam que a presença do aliado em agendas fora do estado agrega valor à candidatura. Antes desta semana, já estiveram juntos em Brasília e Goiás.

Cobrado ao longo do ciclo eleitoral por um engajamento maior na campanha do aliado, o governador de São Paulo prometeu “mergulhar de cabeça” na campanha de Flávio no segundo turno e disse que o ajudaria “até fora do estado”. Em São Paulo, realizaram uma série de agendas conjuntas nos últimos meses.

Na terça (13), estavam lado a lado no evento em que a maior parte dos diretórios do MDB declarou apoio ao candidato , em um encontro com motoboys e em um encontro organizado pela Associação Comercial de São Paulo. Neste último, Flávio afirmou publicamente que Tarcísio tinha expectativa de ser candidato a presidente e que, assim que foi escolhido para concorrer, conversou com o pai sobre visitar o governador no Palácio do Bandeirantes.

O candidato do PL deve voltar no fim de semana a São Paulo para um ato na avenida Paulista em apoio à sua eleição, com participação de outros aliados.

Já Alckmin tem uma agenda intensa prevista para os próximos dias. Nesta quarta (14), em agenda em Niterói com empresários, resumiu a estratégia da campanha para os próximos dias: "Olha, é buscar o voto com humildade. A campanha é curta. Segundo turno são três semanas só. O Brasil é um continente, então a gente se divide: um vai para um lado, o outro vai para o outro", afirmou.

São Paulo, maior colégio eleitoral do país, é um dos focos. Alckmin governou o estado por quatro mandatos, quando ainda era filiado ao PSDB. Na última semana, foi à comunidade de Paraisópolis, onde conversou com moradores. Nesta segunda (12), participou de missa no Santuário Nacional de Aparecida. Deve voltar a São Paulo na sexta (16) para um encontro com médicos na capital e evento com prefeitos em Hortolândia, no interior.

Lula ainda não está confirmado nas agendas no estado. Aliados articulam um ato final no dia 24 de outubro, na avenida Paulista. A última vez em que estiveram juntos foi no ato realizado na mesma avenida no último domingo (11).

Há previsão ainda de agendas de Alckmin no interior de São Paulo, Bahia, Minas Gerais e no Paraná.

Os compromissos vêm na esteira de uma cobrança por um espaço maior do vice na campanha. Em entrevista ao Estúdio i, a ex-senadora e coordenadora de campanha do Lula, Kátia Abreu, defendeu que Alckmin deveria aparecer mais na campanha e destacou a experiência e a capacidade do vice-presidente, principalmente na área econômica, repercutindo críticas feitas durante reunião em Brasília.

Outros aliados de Lula têm realizado agendas e eventos em prol da reeleição do presidente. Fernando Haddad (PT), Marina Silva (Rede) e Simone Tebet (PSB), entre eles, nesta terça (13), participaram de um ato com a militância no Largo da Batata, em Pinheiros, zona oeste de São Paulo.

articles.title: Fim da escala 6x1 também afeta quem trabalha de segunda a sexta | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança prevê redução gradual da jornada para 40 horas semanais e dois dias de descanso remunerado, mas as folgas não precisam ser aos sábados e domingos.
articles.summary: Mudança prevê redução gradual da jornada para 40 horas semanais e dois dias de descanso remunerado, mas as folgas não precisam ser aos sábados e domingos.
articles.body:
A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que prevê o fim da escala 6x1, com dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana, foi aprovada pelo Senado nesta quarta-feira (14).

A proposta recebeu 75 votos favoráveis e um contrário nos dois turnos de votação. O senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS) foi o único a votar contra o texto.

Para acelerar a tramitação, a votação ocorreu em dois turnos no mesmo dia. As novas regras, no entanto, não entram em vigor imediatamente.

Com a aprovação pelo Senado, a emenda constitucional será promulgada em sessão solene do Congresso Nacional, sem precisar passar pela sanção do presidente da República, como ocorre com projetos de lei.

A mudança começa a produzir efeitos após a publicação no Diário Oficial. As novas regras devem começar a valer dois meses após a publicação da emenda constitucional .

A partir desse prazo, os trabalhadores terão direito a dois dias de repouso semanal remunerado , com possibilidade de compensação prevista em norma coletiva, desde que seja assegurada a média de dois dias de descanso por semana.

A proposta também prevê a redução gradual da jornada semanal, sem diminuição salarial. Durante o primeiro ano de transição, o limite será de 42 horas semanais.

Segundo Vivian De Camillis, especialista em direito do trabalho e sócia da área trabalhista do escritório Tilkian Marinelli Marrey, se essa carga horária for distribuída igualmente por cinco dias de trabalho, o empregado cumprirá 8 horas e 24 minutos por dia.

Após um ano de transição, entrará em vigor o limite de 40 horas semanais . Nesse cenário, uma jornada distribuída igualmente por cinco dias corresponderá a oito horas diárias, com dois dias de descanso remunerado .

Redução da jornada também afeta quem já trabalha de segunda a sexta

A mudança também terá impacto para trabalhadores que já cumprem a escala 5x2, de segunda a sexta-feira, com folgas aos sábados e domingos.

Atualmente, quem tem jornada de 44 horas semanais pode trabalhar oito horas de segunda a sexta-feira e mais quatro horas no sábado. Para compensar o sábado, muitas empresas distribuem essas horas ao longo da semana, ampliando a jornada diária.

Com a redução do limite para 40 horas semanais, a compensação das horas correspondentes ao sábado poderá deixar de ser necessária para quem cumprir toda a jornada de segunda a sexta-feira, conforme as condições do contrato e as regras aplicáveis.

“Assim, esses trabalhadores também poderão ter a jornada diária reduzida, sem precisar trabalhar horas a mais durante a semana para compensar o sábado”, explica Vivian De Camillis.

A quantidade de horas trabalhadas por dia dependerá da distribuição da jornada ao longo da semana. Considerando uma divisão igual entre cinco dias de trabalho, os limites ficam assim:

A partir de dois meses da publicação: limite de 42 horas semanais, equivalente a 8 horas e 24 minutos por dia, se a jornada for distribuída igualmente em cinco dias.

Após um ano de transição: limite de 40 horas semanais, equivalente a 8 horas por dia, em cinco dias de trabalho.

A redução para 40 horas semanais, porém, não significa que todos os trabalhadores terão necessariamente a mesma jornada diária . A distribuição das horas poderá variar, respeitadas as regras aplicáveis.

Folgas não precisam ser aos sábados e domingos

O fim da escala 6x1 também tem gerado dúvidas sobre a obrigatoriedade de folgas aos sábados e domingos. A proposta não determina, necessariamente, que os dois dias de descanso coincidam com o fim de semana .

Segundo o advogado trabalhista Antonio Vasconcellos Junior, a proposta estabelece dois descansos semanais remunerados de 24 horas consecutivas , preferencialmente aos sábados e domingos, em linha com a previsão da legislação atual sobre o repouso semanal.

Na prática, isso significa que as folgas podem ocorrer em outros dias da semana. Um trabalhador pode, por exemplo, descansar na terça e na quinta-feira, desde que a escala respeite as regras previstas na norma.

“O essencial é que sejam assegurados dois períodos de descanso semanal, cada um com 24 horas consecutivas, independentemente dos dias em que ocorram”, afirma Vasconcellos Junior, sócio-fundador do AVJ Advogados.

O advogado trabalhista Maurício Corrêa da Veiga complementa que a legislação atual já assegura um descanso semanal de 24 horas, preferencialmente aos domingos, mas não obrigatoriamente nesse dia.

Na prática, a distribuição das folgas poderá variar conforme o setor e o tipo de atividade da empresa , especialmente em áreas que funcionam continuamente, como comércio, saúde e serviços.

articles.title: Exclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say
articles.summary: The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and...
articles.body:
The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called "mother of all bombs" to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter.

Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump's stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said.

Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of US bombing.

While the US military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do.

For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a "definitive" end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans.

While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the US still has unfinished business in the country.

Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring US troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat.

Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn't know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day.

Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include "a lot of energy infrastructure" and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come "prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility)," indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out.

A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain , also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the US and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon.

Another US official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added.

But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran's nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground. While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said.

"The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else," a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. "It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead."

If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb's massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites.

Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While US officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran's capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict's current status quo.

"POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped," the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added.

Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action.

Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting US boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close.

Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a "symbolic" win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported.

A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon's recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a "fireworks show," with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place.

And despite Trump's recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the US military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order.

The next turnover of US troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a US official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members.

Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding "President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."

In response to CNN's request for comment, a Pentagon official said: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."

MOAB developed for 'psychological operations'

Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides.

During the final stages of testing in 2003 , military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for "psychological operations."

Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting.

As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels.

Trump was the first US president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017.

That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and US officials added at the time.

At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump , who advocated an isolationist, "America first" foreign policy during his first election campaign.

Following the 2017 strike, US military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran.

articles.title: Trump touts booming economy at Montana rally, but supporters feel the pinch
articles.summary: KALISPELL, Mont. — On a day when the U.S. inflation rate was shown to have climbed 3.7% over the past year, President Donald Trump said at a rally in Montana on Wednesday, “We have very little inflation.”
articles.body: KALISPELL, Mont. — On a day when the U.S. inflation rate was shown to have climbed 3.7% over the past year, President Donald Trump said at a rally in Montana on Wednesday, “We have very little inflation.” Trump touted a booming economy as he campaigned for Republican candidates on the final leg of a Western campaign swing, three weeks before the midterm elections. Poverty is down and incomes are up, he told the crowd. More than $22 trillion is flowing into the country and with that record-setting level of investment, “they’re building plants all over Montana, and they’re building plants all over …” “Everyone, we’re all having a good time,” he said. Yet the economic resurgence he described isn’t the reality that many people say they are living. In interviews before Trump appeared onstage, some of the supporters who came to see him said they’re feeling squeezed by grocery, housing and fuel costs. Moneen Ahlquist, an 84-year-old homemaker who lives in Missoula, said that she is careful to combine errands in one trip so that she can keep her car in the garage and save on gas. “We shop at grocery stores where we can pump our gas and get a few cents off,” she said. Megan Gurhlke, 44, who works on a dairy farm, said that three of her four family members work full time and yet, “We can’t afford stuff because the prices are so bad.” “I represent the majority of our country,” she said. “We barely make ends meet, but we push to do it.” If there’s encouraging news for Trump in the face of such sentiments, it’s that his supporters don’t believe he’s at fault. Some echoed Trump’s contention that former President Joe Biden is to blame for high prices. Others said that they’re prepared to be patient and wait for Trump’s policies to fully kick in and make life more affordable. “Right now, they [prices] are getting worse,” said Gary Hanson, 67, a hardware store owner in Kalispell. “It’s going to take a long time to turn everything around and that’s what Trump is looking at.” As she stood in line to see the president, Jennifer Piperakis, 53, mentioned that filling her truck with diesel fuel costs her $200. “Gas prices are outrageous,” she said. Still, she said, “I love President Trump. I love what he’s doing for veterans. He’s not about himself. He’s about trying to help. My husband is a veteran. Biden didn’t do anything for him.” Elections often hinge on the economy. Polling suggests that voters’ unhappiness with economic conditions could cost the Republicans their slim congressional majority. Trump’s message as he campaigns across the country is that people aren’t hurting; they’re thriving. In his speech Wednesday, he cited stock market gains that are boosting retirement savings. He nodded to high fuel costs but predicted that they’ll drop once the Iran war ends. Defending the tariffs he’s imposed on foreign countries, he said that they’ve produced considerable wealth. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We’re making more money now there than we ever — and we have more jobs than ever before. Remember that.” As for inflation, he said “we don’t have inflation.”

articles.title: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt opens up about Trump, motherhood
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt called President Trump "the best boss" and revealed details about her grueling work weeks before leaving the White House press role to spend more time with her children.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt offered a glimpse into her relationship with President Donald Trump during a candid Instagram Q&A, praising her former boss as "kind and uplifting" while opening up about personal life decisions. Leavitt, 29, fielded a variety of questions from her Instagram followers while traveling Wednesday, touching on everything from Trump's personality to her career plans and life as a mother of two. When asked whether Trump was nice or kind, Leavitt offered insight into his personality. "Yes! He’s the best boss," she said. LEAVITT PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON TRUMP'S 'TENSE,' UNFILTERED PRIVATE TALKS WITH PUTIN, XI, STARMER "People don’t see this side of him because the media doesn’t show it but he has been nothing but kind and uplifting to me, even since departing," she continued. "He’s also hilarious. Love him!" Leavitt, who served as press secretary from January 2025 until August 2026, also addressed a question about landing another job after her decision to leave the White House to spend more time with her children. "As Press Sec, I was working in the office 60+ hours a week, traveling the world, and always on call 24/7," she said. "Now, I am home with my kids every day and doing some TV hits. These things are not the same, ma’am." KAROLINE LEAVITT INVITED AS A GUEST ON ABC'S 'THE VIEW' AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE ROLE Leavitt also confirmed that she would officially begin working as a Fox News Channel contributor next month. "I will be officially joining Fox News as a TV Contributor on November 1st, so I will continue making appearances on various shows!" she wrote. FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott announced Leavitt's new role earlier this month, and she is expected to provide commentary across the network's programming. Leavitt previously worked in Trump’s first administration as a presidential writer and assistant press secretary before running for Congress as a Republican in New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District in 2022. She also served as communications director for then-House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Elise Stefanik. When asked for career advice for people hoping to succeed in public relations or politics, Leavitt encouraged them to gain practical experience before graduating. KAROLINE LEAVITT ANNOUNCES BIRTH OF SECOND CHILD, A GIRL "My advice to people who want to get into politics or comms is to get real world experience when you're in college," she said. "You'll be taught a lot of things in the classroom, but work experience is where you're really going to learn the game." Leavitt said she interned at NBC Sports Boston because she initially considered becoming a sideline sports reporter. She also worked at a local news station before securing a White House internship. "Just try to apply for internships, say yes to every opportunity that you can and don't spend your summers hanging out, spend your summers working and gaining that real world experience, which will help you later in your career." Leavitt, who made history as the youngest White House press secretary, was also asked how she spends her free time. "I don't have free time. As a mom of two littles, I'm lucky if I can take a shower in peace. But it's the season of life I'm in and I wouldn't have it any other way!!!!" articles.title: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.
articles.body:
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.

President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer.

But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".

Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.

It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".

The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.

A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.

The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.

She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?"

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.

A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.

Watch: How did Katie Zacharia do at her first - very brief - White House briefing?

She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.

Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.

In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.

In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.

The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment, as well as Zhong Lun Law Firm.

It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.

Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

articles.title: Trump unveils newly renovated White House facade: ‘Very proud’
articles.summary: The work comes amid a broader transformation of the White House, including work on the North Portico and the former East Wing.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has shared new images of what he described as the "fully renovated" White House facade, saying extensive restoration work has given the historic building decades of additional life.

Trump posted photographs of the South side of the White House to Truth Social early Thursday, highlighting restoration of the exterior as well as a new South Entrance and helipad.

"Actual pictures of our fully renovated White House facade, facing South, with the new South Entrance, and Heliport!" Trump wrote.

"It had to be done, and I am very proud to be the President who did it!" Trump added.

The work comes amid a much broader transformation of the White House complex during Trump's second term, including work on the North Portico, changes to the Rose Garden and extensive construction on the site of the former East Wing for a new ballroom and military complex.

Trump said Thursday that the ballroom and military complex were "on time, and on budget," describing them as an "unbelievably beautiful addition" to the White House.

The project has been the subject of legal challenges and scrutiny over its cost and funding, with the Supreme Court allowing construction to continue in August while litigation over the project proceeds.

Newsweek has contacted the White House and National Park Service for further comment.

Trump's newly released photographs focus on the South facade, one of the most recognizable views of the White House.

The South Portico, with its curved colonnade and Truman Balcony above it, faces the South Lawn and has historically served as an arrival and departure point for presidents and foreign leaders.

Trump said the work addressed deterioration to both the building's exterior walls and decorative architectural features.

"Over the years, the facade, both North and South, suffered tremendous wear, tear, and damage," he wrote. "The exterior walls and ornamentation, both missing and in bad condition, has been fully restored to the Highest Level, giving the White House many decades of additional life!"

The president did not provide a detailed breakdown of the restoration work or its cost. Work has also been underway on the White House's North Portico. The Washington Post reported in September that workers had spent roughly two months repairing the historic columns and strengthening the entrance before coverings surrounding the structure began to be removed.

The White House itself dates to the 1790s, although the building has repeatedly been rebuilt, expanded and renovated. The South Portico was constructed during James Monroe's presidency in the 1820s, while the North Portico was added several years later under Andrew Jackson. The West Wing was constructed during Theodore Roosevelt's presidency in 1902 and the White House underwent a near-total interior reconstruction during Harry Truman's presidency between 1948 and 1952.

The facade restoration is part of a series of changes Trump has made to the White House and its grounds, among the most significant being the ballroom and associated East Wing redevelopment.

The original East Wing was demolished as the administration moved ahead with plans for a large new ceremonial space and additional security and military infrastructure.

Trump initially promoted the ballroom as a privately funded addition designed to give the White House a permanent space for large state events rather than relying on temporary tents. The project has since expanded to include substantial underground security infrastructure and other facilities.

In August, the Supreme Court permitted construction to continue while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation proceeds. The Court said its ruling did not decide the ultimate legality of the project but found that the government was likely to prevail on its argument that the preservation group lacked standing. Trump has repeatedly said taxpayers will not pay for the ballroom itself.

In September, he said the ballroom would cost close to $400 million and was being funded by himself and private companies. Internal contractor documents reported by The Washington Post , however, estimated the wider East Wing project at about $600 million, with approximately $293 million expected from private sources and the remainder associated with government-funded security, military and Executive Residence work.

The White House has said those taxpayer-funded costs relate to security and other government functions rather than the ballroom itself. Trump reiterated Thursday that the work remained on schedule.

"Likewise, the Ballroom and Military Complex, is on time, and on budget," he wrote.

Trump said the development would be the most significant addition to the White House since the West Wing was constructed.

articles.title: MARK HALPERIN: Republicans are bracing for a wipeout. Here's who they'll blame if it happens
articles.summary: Political strategists on both sides are already rehearsing recriminations weeks before Election Day, preparing to win the argument about why it was lost.
articles.body: The political strategists I have known in my career are among the smartest, most interesting, most knowledgeable and most impressive people I have ever met. They are also capable of more white-hot animus for other people than anyone I have ever met. And I am not talking about Democrats hating Republicans, or vice versa. That is frequently a manageable relationship. Sometimes they even share a corporate client. BATTLEGROUND REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON KEY ISSUES IN FINAL MIDTERM SPRINT The disgust to which I refer is intraparty. That is when the hatred becomes unmatched by all other human relationships. More than Glinda felt pure, unadulterated loathing for Elphaba at the beginning of "Wicked." More than a tenant despises her cruel and unusual landlord. More than the Red Sox detest the Yankees. These folks are experts at circular firing squads and shooting off bazookas inside the tent. Most political strategists detest two things: losing campaigns and losing money. The pair is connected. An election defeat can cost you your next client. Being blamed for an election defeat can cost you several. There is, therefore, a substantial professional incentive to establish that the catastrophe was foreseeable, preventable and definitely somebody else’s doing. With a few weeks to go before Election Day, Democratic strategists are feeling good or great, while Republicans range from uneasy and determined to absolutely horrible. The latter have begun rehearsing their recriminations with select audiences. Some of those audiences are reporters. Most political strategists detest two things: losing campaigns and losing money. The pair is connected. An election defeat can cost you your next client. Being blamed for an election defeat can cost you several. MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE The Democrats will not need a lengthy warm-up period if the election disappoints. There are two parallel campaigns underway: the one to win the election and the one to win the argument about why it was lost. LEE CARTER: TRUMP CAN STILL GET ATTENTION, CAN HE DISTRACT VOTERS FROM THEIR BILLS? On the Republican side, the simplest argument is also the hardest to refute. One man controls the party, and his name is Trump. His advisers can recommend a message, a schedule, a spending plan or a period of blessed silence. They cannot guarantee delivery. A Republican wipeout would thus produce a comprehensive Trump indictment: his unpopularity, his indiscipline, his economic decisions, his foreign entanglements, his family’s enrichment and his apparently inexhaustible interest in attaching his name to things. Trump’s cheerleading for AI and data centers is hurting Republicans, too, alienating voters who see higher electric bills and threats to their jobs where he sees a glorious future. The defense of the staff will be that they could not control him. The prosecution’s response will be that taking responsibility for the consequences of not managing him properly was rather prominently included in the job description. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS There had been a plausible Republican case for optimism late last year. Democrats were divided, the Senate map was favorable, the novel mid-decade redistricting plan seemed to be working, and Republicans could hope voters would tolerate an economic mixed bag if the promised benefits began arriving. Instead, a voter worried about groceries sees a president worried about building names. A family falling behind on retirement savings hears about a ballroom. A young adult unable to afford a house watches the president’s family make deals. IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY Each story supplies the caption for the next one. The political damage requires voters to conclude that the president is spending more time on his surroundings than on theirs. "Why is he focused on a Washington arts building instead of my wallet?" is a question no Republican media buyer can answer with another video invoking Zohran Mamdani or AOC. The Iran conflict compounds the problem: higher energy costs, another foreign war that seems to be taking forever and a president who campaigned on avoiding precisely that sort of entanglement. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune will face a related accusation: that congressional Republicans produced too little voters could feel, understand or remember. A legislative accomplishment that requires a staff briefing to appreciate is difficult to sell in a 30-second spot. ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY: DATA Republicans have money. What they have lacked is a national message persuasive enough to make that money work. The consultants will say the committees commissioned stale spots and recycled attacks, and started airing them too late. If the spots fail, the people who approved them will explain that testing showed they worked. The people who opposed them will explain that they always knew the testing was wrong. The turnout people will be asked why they could not bring Trump-only voters back for an election without Trump on the ballot. The candidate recruiters will be asked why loyalty at times outranked electability. Individual candidates will be blamed for hugging him too tightly or abandoning him too quickly. Some may achieve the distinction of being blamed for both. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY And the media will occupy its customary place in the Republican explanation: burying accomplishments, magnifying liabilities and making every Republican candidate answer for Trump. The Democratic version will be less centered on one man and considerably more crowded. Suppose Democrats barely take the House and fail to win the Senate. What might once have been celebrated as a successful midterm could become an indictment of a party that persuaded itself it was entitled to a much bigger one. Once a wave becomes the assumed outcome, every seat it fails to wash ashore becomes evidence of malpractice. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will be accused of weak leadership. The progressives will say the party offered voters too little to get excited about. The moderates will say the progressives offered Republicans entirely too much to get excited about. Strategists who made Trump the central issue will be accused of neglecting household costs. Strategists who emphasized household costs will be accused of failing to make voters understand the full danger of Trump. Republican billionaires will be accused of buying the final weeks, and their Democratic counterparts will be blamed for sitting on their wallets. The Democratic media complaint will be the inverse of the Republican one: Trump was normalized, and his opponents held to a higher standard. There is no neutral after-action report when the authors are competing for the next contract. That does not make the recriminations worthless. Sometimes the angriest person understands the failure best. Political strategists are very good at spotting other political strategists’ mistakes. They are less consistent about spotting their own. articles.title: MORNING GLORY: The polls got Michigan badly wrong. Now Democrats may face a bigger reckoning
articles.summary: Here's why Abdul El-Sayed's ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker and his refusal to call Israel an ally over Iran could cost him the Michigan Senate race against Mike Rogers.
articles.body: The nationwide duel for the Senate is going on in the dark because polling this year has produced a series of spectacular busts, especially in Michigan, where polls on the primary battle between Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens posted double-digit lead after double-digit lead for El-Sayed. In fact, El-Sayed won by 1% — not the 10-18% that had been predicted. It turns out those polls may have suppressed voter turnout and encouraged some Stevens voters to stay home. It is doubtful anyone following the news will stay home in Michigan in the general election. El-Sayed is — at best! — an Islamist apologist. He cannot own his past statements or campaign rhetoric. He refuses to discuss his most prominent supporter in the primary: far-left streamer and YouTube personality Hasan Piker, who is part crazy and part extremist. Piker carried El-Sayed over the finish line in the primary, but now voters are supposed to accept El-Sayed’s deflections when questioned about him. HISTORIC NEWSPAPER GIVES EL-SAYED A SAVAGE REBUKE FOR HIDING HIS PAST WHILE ENDORSING HIS OPPONENT El-Sayed is a radical. He’s done very little to hide his antipathy toward America’s ally Israel, going so far as to equate Israel with the Islamic Republic of Iran. Iran has, of course, been at war with the United States since its revolution in 1979. That regime is responsible for the deaths of more than a thousand Americans, whether blown up at the U.S. Embassy or the Marine Corps barracks in Beirut in 1983 by Iran’s proxy in Lebanon, Hezbollah, or this past weekend, when another American was killed by another Iranian proxy, the Houthis, via a Houthi missile attack on the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Still, El-Sayed cannot simply declare that Israel is our ally and Iran is our enemy. That should tell everyone all they need to know about El-Sayed and cost him on November 3. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER All across the country, Democrats have nominated candidates from the fringe, from El-Sayed in Michigan to James Talarico in Texas, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Troy Jackson in Maine. It’s as though the Democratic National Committee put zero effort into candidate recruitment, or maybe they just threw darts at a board marked with "Guaranteed to Lose" at the top. But El-Sayed is the worst of the lot … by a lot. And the stories keep coming as opposition research reveals facts about El-Sayed’s past that he has tried to hide, including his claim of dual citizenship, which he has subsequently repudiated. With nearly three weeks left before polls close, it’s fair to expect that more such old tape and tweets will surface. FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY' El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, is, by contrast, a mainstream and moderate Michigander, a former FBI agent and lieutenant in the Army before he went on to serve in the Michigan legislature and then for more than a decade in the House of Representatives, finishing there as chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. (That’s significant, by the way, as the Intelligence Committee is a select committee, with members selected by the speaker and the House minority leader, traditionally because of their national security chops.) Rogers v. El-Sayed ought not to be close. And chances are it won’t be because of El-Sayed’s reported difficulty connecting with Detroit’s Black community, on which Democrats traditionally rely to win in the Wolverine State. ROGERS OPENS DOOR TO DEMOCRATIC VOTERS AFTER EL-SAYED’S PRIMARY VICTORY: ‘THERE IS STILL HOPE’ Report after report hints at the long-standing estrangement between the Black and Arab American communities in and around Detroit, but hardly any pollster knows how to account for the antipathy felt toward El-Sayed by Black voters. Campaign drop-bys by former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama are as close to "break glass, pull alarm" emergency signals as you can get, but they are not doing the trick. BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE' The trouble? Traditional Democrats know El-Sayed. He’s run for political office before. And lost before. "Winsome and gracious" is not on his resume. If anything, he’s the angriest major-party candidate we’ve seen in decades. His refusal to answer basic questions about Piker, about his family’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and about the impact of "Medicare for All" on union-negotiated health care plans (the former would destroy the latter) marks El-Sayed as untrustworthy. An early call for Rogers on election night will secure the Senate majority for Republicans. (That result might have already been accomplished by victories for Sens. Susan Collins in Maine and John Sununu in New Hampshire, but Rogers getting the call early on November 3 would be a great relief.) CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Beyond simply having the far better man win an election, though, the victory of Rogers over El-Sayed will be a win for moderation and maturity and a rejection of the sort of extremism that Democrats have not flirted with outside of the deep-blue urban districts that sent AOC, Ilhan Omar and the rest of "The Squad" to D.C. Losing the Democrats to the control of extremists like El-Sayed would be terrible for everyone, including, and most especially, the Democratic Party. articles.title: Press freedom groups that blasted Trump turn fire on Dem governor over alleged media retaliation
articles.summary: Press freedom groups that have condemned Trump's treatment of journalists are now comparing outspoken Trump critic Wes Moore's media practices to those of the president.
articles.body: A coalition of prominent press freedom organizations that have blasted President Donald Trump's treatment of journalists is now accusing Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Trump critic himself, of retaliating against news outlets scrutinizing his administration. The accusations came in an Oct. 13 letter from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and six other journalism and civil liberties organizations. The groups raised concerns about the Moore administration's decision to subject even routine inquiries from reporters at Sinclair-affiliated news outlets and The Baltimore Sun to additional legal review. The additional review came amid a defamation lawsuit filed against Moore by David Smith, executive chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group and majority owner of The Baltimore Sun. Maryland agencies have explicitly cited Smith's lawsuit in written responses to reporters, informing journalists at Sinclair-affiliated outlets that their inquiries would be referred to legal counsel before receiving a response. Moore himself has previously criticized Trump's treatment of journalists. During a Sept. 20 appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," the Maryland governor condemned the president's decision to bar reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing Trump of treating the Constitution "like it is a suggestion box simply because he does not like the coverage." WHITE HOUSE WON'T BACK DOWN AS ATTORNEY PREDICTS HOW TRUMP'S LATEST PRESS TUSSLE WILL PLAY OUT IN COURT "It's particularly offensive that Moore seeks to boost his national profile by slamming the Trump administration's unconstitutional attempts to ban disfavored media outlets from the White House when he's engaged in such similar antics himself," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement accompanying the letter. The press freedom groups that joined in condemning Moore, including the Committee to Protect Journalists, PEN America, Reporters Without Borders and the Society of Professional Journalists, argued that journalists should not face different treatment from government officials because of a dispute involving their outlets' ownership, drawing a comparison to the Trump administration's restrictions on certain White House reporters. Moore's office strongly disputed the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital on Wednesday, insisting that reporters have continued receiving responses from state agencies despite the additional legal scrutiny. BALTIMORE SUN OWNER THREATENS MD GOV WES MOORE WITH LAWSUIT OVER WHAT HE CALLS A DEFAMATORY EPSTEIN LINK "The central premise of this letter is completely false. There is no blanket refusal to engage," Ammar Moussa, Moore's senior press secretary and director of media strategy, told Fox News Digital. "In the last week alone, state agencies and the Governor's Office have answered dozens of questions from Sinclair outlets, and we're happy to let them share those responses." "David Smith chose to sue the Governor. Having our legal team look over inquiries is basic due diligence, not a blackout," Moussa continued. "A litigant doesn't get to dictate how the state protects itself, but that hasn't stopped our agencies from doing their jobs for the people of Maryland." The dispute traces back to a defamation lawsuit Smith filed against the governor in July. Smith accused Moore of making false and damaging statements about him during a television interview, including remarks Smith interpreted as suggesting he had ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Smith, whose media holdings include The Baltimore Sun, has been a frequent target of criticism from Moore, who has accused the newspaper's ownership of advancing a political agenda aligned with Trump. Smith maintains that the governor's remarks crossed the line from political criticism into defamation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The lawsuit was filed by Smith personally, rather than the news organizations whose reporters have since faced additional legal review of their inquiries. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "We urge you to instruct all Maryland agencies that Smith’s lawsuit against you is a personal matter and not an excuse to send media requests into a legal review black hole, and to cease any other unlawful retaliation against news outlets you personally dislike," the coalition letter stated. "It is particularly jarring that, while government agencies under your watch stonewall reporters based on flimsy pretexts, you take to the airwaves to condemn the Trump administration’s unconstitutional ban of news outlets the president doesn’t like from the White House," the letter continued. "Yes, Trump frequently turns his personal grudges into censorial government policy, to the detriment of the public. But your own conduct appears not much different."

articles.title: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
articles.summary: More than 12,000 people filled a major venue in the city to hear the former US president's take on the challenges the world is facing. .
articles.body:
Barack Obama has told an audience in Glasgow that hope is worth fighting for despite big challenges facing the modern world.

The 44th president of the United States said online platforms had shifted in recent years to focus on content that stoked anger and fear, but he believes a drift to extremism is "not inevitable".

The comments came as he addressed an OVO Hydro crowd of 12,150 people while in conversation with British journalist and author Sathnam Sanghera, part of three speaking dates in the UK.

He reflected on his time in the White House and examined the political and social challenges facing the US and the wider world.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope

But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.

He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill".

"It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said.

"So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."

But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".

He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler.

"We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'."

Obama, who was president until 2016, said there was a "critical balance" that must be struck between free speech and regulation.

But the 65-year-old said that the world and its leaders are going to need to find mechanisms and new institutions to allow rigorous debate and disagreement while helping people sort out basic facts.

He said: "If I had a blame pie for why politics is so polarised and why we're seeing a rise of populism in many places, it's because of that information that is going into our brains every day."

Obama said this resulted in young people feeling discouraged, and that "it's not a healthy diet that our brains are on at the moment".

He added that he feared this could become even worse with AI making it hard to distinguish between what is true and what is not, something he believes will make democracy hard to function.

Obama says people forget lessons from the past

Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.

The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.

He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet."

He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible.

"I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.

Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted.

"We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."

He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.

Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.
