articles.title: Georgia voters set early-voting record as midterm elections heat up
articles.summary: Brad Raffensperger praised record Georgia early voting turnout as the fiery Jon Ossoff and Mike Collins Senate debate exploded over personal attacks.
articles.body: Over 180,000 Georgians cast their ballots on the first day of early voting on Tuesday, setting a record for midterm elections. Tuesday's total eclipsed the first day of early voting in 2022 by more than 55,000 votes, state election officials say. Georgia's early voting schedule runs through Oct. 30. "This record-breaking turnout proves that voters have confidence in the integrity of our elections," Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said in a statement. "It’s a testament to our strong election system overseen by 159 of the best county election officials in the country." Georgia's contentious U.S. Senate race erupted into a heated confrontation Tuesday night as Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., accused GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., of allowing the dissemination of "neo-Nazi propaganda" inside his own home, prompting Collins to fire back over Ossoff's financial support from a billionaire with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY The exchange unfolded during the candidates' second and final debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, which was hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and broadcast by Georgia Public Broadcasting network. ANTISEMITISM FIGHT EXPLODES IN FLORIDA AS VOTERS HEAD TO THE POLLS: 'POLITICAL POGROM' During the debate, Ossoff sought to tie his GOP opponent to White nationalism and repeatedly demanded that Collins commit to stopping the dissemination of hateful rhetoric involving his campaign staff, in particular Collins' son-in-law, which Ossoff alleged had continued despite blowback. "How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for the Senate?" Ossoff asked, referencing reporting about his opponent's son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, who was the subject of a CNN investigation about sharing Nazi propaganda imagery, promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories and polling his online followers about whether he should produce a video titled, "Why Gen-Z Doesn't Hate Hitler." FORMER HOUSE INTEL LEADER POINTS TO DEM RHETORIC 'ENCOURAGING' VIOLENCE; EIGHTH MAN CHARGED IN UFC TERROR PLOT Meanwhile, Collins accused his Democrat opponent of fueling threats against his family and refusing to return campaign support connected to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, He also questioned Ossoff over his support for candidates linked to controversial streamer Hasan Piker. ‘MISLEADING VOTERS’: OSSOFF WARNS DONORS HE’S FALLING BEHIND DESPITE LEADING SENATE FUNDRAISING "I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "There's a crazy person in jail right now because of your rhetoric," he alleged, before saying he had received another threat just the previous day. "Why don't you denounce that? Why don't you return that money?" Fox News' Alec Schemmel contributed to this report.

articles.title: Donald Trump estudia usar la MOAB, madre de todas las bombas, contra Irán: 10.000 kilos y poder explosivo de once toneladas de TNT
articles.standfirst: Estados Unidos contempla atacar de forma contundente su infraestructura energética
articles.summary: Estados Unidos contempla atacar de forma contundente su infraestructura energética
articles.body: El conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Irán no cesa. El ejército estadounidense no descarta, según fuentes consultadas por la CNN, utilizar la denominada MOAB para atacar su infraestructura energética y nuclear. Las siglas MOAB responden a Massive Ordnance Air Blast y es conocida popularmente como la madre de todas las bombas. Estos planes de ataque, de concretarse, supondrían un punto de inflexión en el conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Irán, según analiza la CNN. El citado medio mantiene que Donald Trump está siendo presionado para finalizar el conflicto y sus asesores califican el uso de la MOAB como un paso "definitivo". Todo apunta, de todos modos, a que desde la Casa Blanca no realizarán cambios bruscos de rumbo hasta que se celebren las elecciones de medio mandato (mid-term election), el próximo 3 de noviembre. La CNN, tras hablar con varios funcionarios conocedores de la situación, señala que algunos de ellos no consideran que usar la MOAB sea realmente eficaz para acabar con la infraestructura nuclear de Irán. Pese a su gran poder destructivo, no tendría, según estas fuentes, capacidad de penetración suficiente para acabar con determinadas instalaciones. Más allá de su eficacia desde el punto de vista militar, el citado medio plantea que el uso de este armamento podría servir a Estados Unidos para lanzar un mensaje simbólico a Irán. El último conflicto bélico entre ambos territorios se inició el pasado mes de febrero de este año. La MOAB, o GBU-43/B, es la bomba no atómica más potente del arsenal de Estados Unidos. Pesa 10.000 kilos, su diámetro de explosión es de 1,4 kilómetros y su poder destructivo equivale a once toneladas de TNT. El ejército estadounidense la utilizó por primera vez en un escenario bélico real en abril de 2017. Entonces, Donald Trump también era el inquilino de la Casa Blanca y la usó en Afganistán contra el Estado Islámico.

articles.title: Read this before you buy the ‘blue tsunami’ hype
articles.summary: The news is awash these days with poll-inspired expectations about Democrats winning big in next month’s midterm elections. USA Today declared the other day that “the expected blue wave could be even bigger than expected, and could not only give Democrats control of the House, but also the Senate.” Even more expansively, Huffington Post proclaimed:…
articles.body:
The news is awash these days with poll-inspired expectations about Democrats winning big in next month’s midterm elections . USA Today declared the other day that “the expected blue wave could be even bigger than expected, and could not only give Democrats control of the House, but also the Senate.” Even more expansively, Huffington Post proclaimed : “Historic victories are seemingly within grasp” for Democrats.

And yet, solid reasons exist for treating such poll-based narratives cautiously, even warily, given that surveys are inherently fragile instruments for measuring an ephemeral electorate. As data journalist Nate Silver has noted , “It’s not unreasonable to approach election polls from a position of mild — maybe even more-than-mild — skepticism.”

This is not to say poll-driven expectations are bound for error . They might be accurate; the Democrats might enjoy a “ blue tsunami ” of electoral success next month.

But there are compelling reasons for tempering pre-election headiness — reasons that are rooted in polling’s checkered past. The following summary of recent shortcomings in election polling offers context and justification for tapping the brakes about poll-driven high hopes this year.

Election polls have been underestimating Republicans

Pollsters in 2024 underestimated Donald Trump’s popular support for the third successive presidential election . His vote totals increased in each of the three races, from almost 63 million in 2016 to about 74 million in 2020 to more than 77.3 million in 2024.

Of course, Trump is not on the ballot in 2026, but he has encouraged midterm voters to “close their eyes and pretend” that he is, symbolically.

The hypothesis is that Trump’s presence on the ballot attracts participation by Republicans who otherwise might not vote. But the problem of underestimating Republican turnout goes beyond the Trump candidacies.

More broadly, polls collectively have overstated support for Democratic candidates in five of the past six national elections, according to data posted by Scott Clement, polling director for The Washington Post. If the midterm polls this year systematically overestimate support for Democratic candidates by an average of 3 percentage points, Clement wrote, Democrats likely will win the House but fail to gain control of the Senate.

Pollsters with exceptional records for accuracy have still been known to err dramatically. Reputation brings no insulation from polling embarrassment . This reality has been apparent since the presidential election of 1936 , when Literary Digest magazine — the acknowledged polling oracle of its day — predicted Republican Alf Landon would easily defeat President Franklin D. Roosevelt. The Digest’s projection was based on its huge mail-in poll, which understated Roosevelt’s popular support by nearly 20 percentage points. Landon lost in a landslide, carrying just two states.

More recently, J. Ann Selzer, whose previously stellar survey work won for her acclamation as the “ queen of polling ” and “ best pollster in politics ,” erred dramatically in 2024. Her final Iowa poll before the presidential election said Democrat Kamala Harris had “ clearly leaped into a leading position ” and was 3 points ahead of Trump in the Hawkeye State. The poll result was as stunning as it was unexpected . All but overlooked in the frenzy were results of a concurrent survey by Emerson College that showed Trump leading in Iowa by 10 percentage points.

In the end, Trump carried the state by 13 points , which meant Selzer’s poll was off by 16 points. Soon afterward, Selzer made known her plans to quit election polling. “Polling is a science of estimation,” she said , “and science has a way of periodically humbling the scientist.”

Election polls commissioned or conducted by major news organizations unsurprisingly attract wide attention. The results are promptly shared with large audiences of viewers and readers. But for all their prominence, media polls can be problematic.

In 2024, swing-state polling late in the campaign by CNN, The New York Times/Siena College , and Marist College for PBS and NPR all had Harris leading in enough swing states to win the Electoral College. Had those media polls aligned with election outcomes in swing states, Harris would have been elected president.

Trump carried all seven swing states, if by narrow margins in some of them.

CNN and the Times/Siena poll estimated the race nationally was tied at campaign’s end. Marist estimated that Harris led nationally by 4 points . Trump won the national popular vote by 1.5 points .

The midterm elections four years ago were expected to produce a “ red wave ” of Republican gains in Congress. The political landscape looked bleak for Democrats in the fall of 2022. Inflation was raging then at 7.7 percent , unlawful cross-border migration was surging , and President Biden’s approval rating was down to 40 percent.

The red wave never materialized . Democrats scored a net gain of one Senate seat and kept control of the upper chamber. Republicans picked up just nine seats in the House , enough to give them a wobbly majority.

The better-than-expected outcome for Democrats contributed to Biden’s ill-fated decision to seek reelection in 2024. Biden won all the Democratic presidential primaries that year but quit the campaign in July 2024 following a disastrous debate against Trump.

Polls overall missed the margins of victory by 4 percentage points or more in key Senate races in Arizona, Colorado, Florida, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Washington. In New Hampshire, Democrat Maggie Hassan exceeded the RealClearPolitics polling average by nearly 8 points . In Washington state, Democratic Sen. Patty Murray outperformed the polls by 11 points.

None of this, of course, is to say that election polling’s flawed past is necessarily prologue. But it is reasonable to be braced for surprises, as polls might not offer an accurate indication about elections outcomes.

As the late polling innovator Warren Mitofsky once said about placing excessive confidence in survey data, “There’s a lot of room for humility in polling. Every time you get cocky, you lose.”

W. Joseph Campbell is a professor emeritus at American University in Washington, D.C. His seven solo-authored books include “ Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in U.S. Presidential Elections .”

articles.title: Trump team seeks to push back BBC deposition until January 2027
articles.summary: President Trump’s legal team is seeking to push back testimony by the commander in chief in his lawsuit against the BBC until early next year. In a filing lawyers for the BBC made in court this week, the outlet’s legal team said it had attempted several times this summer to agree on a date for…
articles.body:
President Trump’s legal team is seeking to push back testimony by the commander in chief in his lawsuit against the BBC until early next year.

In a filing lawyers for the BBC made in court this week, the outlet’s legal team said it had attempted several times this summer to agree on a date for deposition with Trump’s lawyers.

After the two sides initially agreed to have the president give testimony this month, the BBC wrote, Trump’s team later notified them “the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance” and that counsel would “endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week,” but a replacement date has not been given.

Last month, Trump’s attorneys notified the BBC legal team that the “Plaintiff would make himself available for a deposition in the second or third week of January 2027” but did not provide any specific date, according to the filing .

Trump is suing the BBC for defamation in connection with a documentary it aired about his efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his comments before the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by his supporters.

The president’s lawyers argue the BBC deceptively edited footage of Trump’s speech to omit him telling a crowd gathered in Washington, D.C., that day to march “peacefully and patriotically” to the Capitol.

The BBC apologized for the edit and ousted a number of editorial leaders in the wake of the lawsuit.

But the outlet has sought to challenge the president’s defamation claim, asking the court earlier this year to allow it to issue subpoenas to Trump family members and examine financial records as part of its legal defense.

articles.title: Democrats must not take their opportunity to win the midterms for granted
articles.summary: Opinion polls aren’t infallible.
articles.body:
Opinion polls suggest Democrats have a good chance of winning control of the House and Senate in midterm elections already underway with early and mail voting. But opinion polls aren’t infallible.

President Trump’s surprise victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 should remind us that polls and pundits can be wrong.

My fellow Democrats shouldn’t assume that a blue wave will sweep away Republican majorities in both congressional chambers or wash the red tide of supermajorities in state houses which we have abandoned in multiple presidential seasons.

Democrats need to mount an all-out get-out-the-vote effort from now through Election Day to flip the House and Senate — a strong get out the vote campaign, followed by a post-election defense of Democratic victories that may be challenged by Republicans.

And while frequent and occasional Democratic voters are as vital as a roux in a creole gumbo recipe, the Democrats need extra seasoning this fall.

We must reach out to independents and Republicans who are disgusted by Trump’s repudiation of traditional Republican positions on a broad range of issues, and by his extremism, incompetence, dishonesty, corruption and failure to deliver on many of his 2024 campaign promises.

As a first step, Democrats still have time to educate voters so they understand the rules governing registration, voter identification and ballot access in their states. Requirements vary across the country. Voters should consult reliable, state-specific information before heading to the polls. That is available here.

Democrats should also encourage voters to cast their ballots early by mail or in person. Bad weather, illness, a heavy workload, traffic jams, long lines at polling places and other unexpected factors can prevent some voters from casting ballots in person on Election Day. Where permitted by law, campaigns and civic organizations should assist voters who need help in returning ballots by mail or in drop boxes.

For years, Republicans and conservative allies have built formidable Election Day turnout operations, relying on volunteers at the precinct level and extensive organizing in the weeks leading up to an election. Democrats must match that intensity.

Pro-democracy organizations, including the No Kings movement, are working to boost voter turnout nationwide. As No Kings says on its website : “Power belongs to the people, but only if we use it.”

Democrats would be wise to strengthen their own field operations while working alongside civic organizations that encourage voting. These efforts will be especially important in reaching young voters and people who often don’t vote.

Infrequent voters should be encouraged to check their registration status now. Voters should confirm their polling locations, learn their state’s deadlines and requirements and make a concrete plan to cast their ballots. The group Vote411 provides voters with useful information on its website about how to make a plan to vote.

Unfortunately, Democrats must prepare for the possibility that Trump and his allies will challenge election results, spread disinformation and sow division when Republican candidates lose.

The Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol by Trump supporters trying to stop Congress from certifying Joe Biden’s legitimate victory remains a sobering reminder of the importance of respect for the will of the voters and a peaceful transfer of power.

Democrats must be ready to respond to Republican attempts to undermine confidence in legitimate election results, while ensuring that every challenge to Democratic victories is addressed through lawful procedures and established safeguards. Democrats must also remain attentive to changes in election administration and redistricting that could affect the competitiveness of congressional races. The integrity of our elections depends on fair rules, transparent procedures and public confidence in the results.

Trump wants us to believe that any election he loses, and many elections lost by Republicans he supports, must be rigged. This is not true.

I have campaigned for Democrats for decades, served twice as interim chair of the Democratic National Committee and remain a member of the DNC. I have never tried to rig an election, and I don’t know any Democrat who has.

Even outstanding candidates can lose elections. I’ve seen this happen many times to Democrats I supported, such as when Vice President Kamala Harris ran for president against Trump in 2024.

I know Harris would have made a great president, but like her, I accepted the judgment of American voters who returned Trump to office. Unless candidates run unopposed, all elections have to end with losers as well as winners.

America has a long tradition of elections administered by Democratic and Republican state and local officials. Protecting that tradition is a responsibility that transcends party. It is what makes our country exceptional and the leader of the free world.

So, my final bit of advice is for Americans of every political persuasion: Believe in our democracy and in free and fair elections.

As former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said in 1947 , two years after his Conservative Party lost an election that removed him from office: “No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise. Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.”

Donna Brazile is a political strategist, a contributor to ABC News and former chair of the Democratic National Committee. She is the author of “ Hacks: Inside the Break-ins and Breakdowns That Put Donald Trump in the White House .”

articles.body:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) went after the Trump administration on Wednesday over the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), who recently had her home raided .

“Me and Ilhan Omar are far apart policy wise. I’m pro life, she’s pro abortion. I’m pro [Second Amendment], she’s pro gun control. And on and on,” Greene said in a post on the social platform X on Wednesday night.

“But can someone tell me how pretending to get ready to deport Ilhan Omar is going to bring gas down under $2, make health insurance freaking affordable, make a family’s weekly grocery bill make sense, and stop sending our beloved military off to fight for another f—ing foreign war???” Greene, who was once a strong Trump supporter but is now a critic, added. “People are so sick and tired of the bulls—.”

On Monday morning , federal agents searched Omar’s home in an ongoing criminal probe. Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out the search, a Justice Department spokesperson told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the Justice Department said in the statement.

Omar blasted the raid on social media, referring to it as “political intimidation.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on X. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the federal investigation targeting Omar has a goal of removing her American citizenship and deporting her from the country, U.S. officials and sources familiar with the matter told the outlet.

“When you dumb mf’ers at the WH actually release the Epstein files and lock up the pedophiles and rapists you all hang out with, then we will start paying attention,” Greene said in her Wednesday post.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department and White House for comment.

articles.title: Talarico on ‘crazy’ conspiracy theories: ‘I learned … that I had died’
articles.summary: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) on Wednesday responded to the “crazy” conspiracy theories that circulated during his time away from the campaign trail with the flu, saying he learned of one rumor “that I had died.” CNN’s Erin Burnett asked Talarico about the theories during a town hall event, asking if the flu was…
articles.body:
Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) on Wednesday responded to the “crazy” conspiracy theories that circulated during his time away from the campaign trail with the flu , saying he learned of one rumor “that I had died.”

CNN’s Erin Burnett asked Talarico about the theories during a town hall event , asking if the flu was the “only reason” he stepped away from campaigning. The Democrat laughed and said “yes,” later adding that his absence “sent my opponent [Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton] and his conspiracy theorists spiraling.”

“I opened up social media and learned that I apparently had dropped out of the race, had flown to a mental hospital in Ohio, that I had died,” he continued. “This is crazy. I mean, these false claims got millions of views online, and this is an example of what I call the rage economy.”

Talarico added that conspiracy theorists “can post anything they want on the internet. They get clicks. The billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry, and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table.”

One of these unfounded rumors included that the Democratic candidate checked into a psychiatric facility in Ohio, with right-wing influencer Nick Sortor on Sunday accusing the candidate’s flu diagnosis of being a “ BIG FAT LIE .”

Talarico spokesperson J.T. Ennis wrote on social platform X that this was “a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory.”

Late last month, the Senate candidate said he felt “kind of under the weather” before learning he had the flu, staying at his Austin, Texas, home while remotely tuning in to a U.S. Hispanic Business Council forum to talk to prospective voters on Sept. 30.

His absence on the campaign trail led Paxton and President Trump to question where the Democrat was . The Republican candidate launched attack ads against Talarico for his pause in campaigning.

“No one has seen him for an extended period of time,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last Wednesday. “Where is he? What is wrong with him? Bad rumors are coming out.”

The president continued, “He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!”

But Talarico has accepted at least four debate invitations from CNN and local TV stations, The Texas Tribune reported . He challenged Paxton to a Fox News debate while speaking at the annual Texas Tribune Festival last month, and Burnett said CNN extended an invitation for the state attorney general to appear at Wednesday’s town hall.

The only debate scheduled for Texas candidates is in the race for railroad commissioner between Democrat Jon Rosenthal and Republican Bo French, a debate Rosenthal confirmed in late September. The forum has not been publicly confirmed by French, however, according to the Tribune.

articles.title: Talarico says Biden ‘failed’ Texas by not securing border
articles.summary: Texas Senate hopeful James Talarico (D) raised criticism of the Biden administration’s immigration policies during a town hall Wednesday evening. The Democratic nominee branded himself as a “border security Democrat” during the event, which was hosted by CNN and Jubilee. “Both political parties have failed us on this issue,” he told the crowd in Fort…
articles.body:
Texas Senate hopeful James Talarico (D) raised criticism of the Biden administration’s immigration policies during a town hall Wednesday evening.

The Democratic nominee branded himself as a “border security Democrat” during the event , which was hosted by CNN and Jubilee.

“Both political parties have failed us on this issue,” he told the crowd in Fort Worth, Texas. “Joe Biden failed us during his administration by not securing the border.”

The candidate added that he disagreed with some of the tactics used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers amid President Trump’s crackdown on immigration in the state.

“ICE should be focused on going after the cartels, not our communities,” the Democrat said.

“They should be going after violent gang members, not moms and babies,” Talarico continued. “And so, I think we’ve got to get to a place where we reject the extremism on this issue in both parties and finally pass comprehensive immigration reform.”

The Senate hopeful also said he would not support abolishing ICE , a position adopted by many progressive Democrats.

“We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that’s not what we’re seeing,” he said. “What we’ve seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that’s what we don’t want in this country.”

The candidate specifically referenced the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by an ICE officer in Houston in July and said he would “fight” for justice for people like Araujo if elected to Congress.

More broadly, Talarico expressed his openness to breaking with his party in the greater interest of the state during the Wednesday remarks.

“I’m a proud Democrat, but I already have a religion , and I already have a sports team, so I have no problem sharing hard truths with my party if it’s what’s best for Texas,” he said.

Talarico’s Trump-backed opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), has declined to participate in debates against the state representative. The Republican nominee lists border security as one of his platforms on his campaign website , pledging to support the completion of the president’s border wall if he wins in November.

Immigration has remained top of mind for many voters in the border state headed into the midterm elections. A recent Fox News poll , conducted at the end of September, showed 47 percent of likely Texas voters believe immigration is “extremely important” to their midterm vote. Paxton had a 20-point advantage among voters in this group.

Additionally, a separate survey from The New York Times/Siena University found 12 percent of likely voters in the state said immigration was their top issue in the election — the second most selected issue area behind affordability.

In the Times/Siena poll, 51 percent of respondents said they would vote for Talarico in November, while 45 percent supported Paxton.

articles.title: Trump’s new sanctions could dismantle the International Criminal Court
articles.summary: On Oct. 9, in the clearest escalation to date of its contempt for the rule of law, the administration sanctioned the court.
articles.body:
Survivors of mass atrocities often face tremendous obstacles when seeking justice. They deserve to know that their suffering matters, that their stories will be heard and that accountability remains possible. Our work reflects a deep moral commitment to help ensure that victims are not left to carry their burdens alone.

However, crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide are often perpetrated by people with power, who seek every opportunity to evade, influence or crush judicial processes. The International Criminal Court stands out as one of the few venues where survivors can turn for accountability when all other avenues are blocked.

And now the Trump administration is seeking to cut off that avenue, too. On Oct. 9, in the clearest escalation to date of its contempt for the rule of law, the administration sanctioned the court. This move could put the court out of business altogether, taking with it the hopes of victims around the globe.

To protect victims’ access to justice, my organization, Human Rights Watch, together with the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights and the Open Society Institute, are challenging the Trump administration’s sanctions before a U.S. court.

The sanctions follow from a 2025 Trump executive order authorizing financial sanctions on International Criminal Court officials and non-U.S. citizens and organizations that work with the International Criminal Court in cases his administration opposes. Under U.S. law, anyone in the U.S. who engages with sanctioned individuals or organizations is subject to severe financial penalties or even lengthy prison sentences.

We are challenging that order, calling on the U.S. court to block the entire sanctions regime . In a blatant abuse of power, Trump has labeled the court’s independent investigations a “ national emergency ,” citing its case against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Even before this escalation, three leading Palestinian human rights organizations, a top human rights expert at the United Nations and judges and prosecutors from the court are under U.S. sanctions.

The result has been restrictions on human rights work, a chilling effect on civil society and a direct threat to the critical work of the International Criminal Court. In addition to Palestine , the court has investigated heinous crimes in such wide-ranging places as the Philippines , Uganda , Sudan , Afghanistan and Ukraine .

Sanctioned individuals and groups have experienced frozen or closed bank accounts, loss of digital services and travel restrictions. The widened sanctions will only create additional harm.

As outrageous as it is that an independent court and respected international judges and prominent human rights defenders are being punished for advancing the cause of justice, the harm reaches far beyond the International Criminal Court and the people named on the sanctions list.

Our organizations work for human rights, justice and accountability in the U.S. and around the world, often in coalition. As the sanctions have been imposed, we have been forced to suspend our work with sanctioned parties. This has hampered our ability to provide legal representation to victims of war crimes, make submissions to the International Criminal Court and collaborate with the sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups on critical research, advocacy, humanitarian aid and human rights monitoring.

When organizations can’t coordinate or collaborate with one another, it harms our ability to advocate for the rights and dignity of the most vulnerable.

Only a couple of years ago, Congress, on a bipartisan basis, acted to support the International Criminal Court in its investigation of egregious crimes in Ukraine. But if justice is legitimate and welcomed only selectively, it is not justice. The rule of law requires acting based on evidence and legal standards, not power or political allegiance.

The court is not a perfect institution; no court is. Civil society organizations have often been among its most persistent critics , with a view toward ensuring that it lives up to its essential mandate. But engaging with the court — or critiquing it — is well within our constitutional and international human rights.

Let’s be clear: The First Amendment does not protect speech only when the government approves of the message or the messenger. Freedom of association means nothing if a president can punish U.S. citizens for associating with individuals and organizations with whom the U.S. government does not agree.

When people and organizations cannot communicate or associate freely, silence takes the place of accountability. Today, the target is support for justice before the International Criminal Court. Tomorrow, it could be work to end corruption, election abuses, torture, political imprisonment or other issues the U.S. government would prefer to keep beyond scrutiny.

That is why our organizations, with different histories, missions and constituencies, have come together in this case.

The question raised by this executive order is larger than the International Criminal Court itself and larger than any single political situation or conflict. It is a question of whether we believe all victims of atrocities deserve justice.

And it is a question of whether people in the U.S. remain free to work for justice when that work is politically inconvenient to those in power.

That is a freedom that is worth defending.

Liz Evenson is international justice director at Human Rights Watch .

articles.title: ICE rejects push for automatically activated body cameras
articles.summary: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) resisted a recommendation from a government watchdog to use automated body camera activation that would engage when a weapon is drawn. A Wednesday report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reviewed ICE’s deployment of body cameras after historic levels of funding were funneled to the immigration agency. The report,…
articles.body:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) resisted a recommendation from a government watchdog to use automated body camera activation that would engage when a weapon is drawn.

A Wednesday report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reviewed ICE’s deployment of body cameras after historic levels of funding were funneled to the immigration agency.

The report, requested by congressional Democrats, comes as they have fumed about slow deployment of the cameras as well as ICE officers’ failure to activate them in a string of shootings, including during multiple fatal interactions. ICE officers have killed six people since President Trump took office.

“ICE has not implemented controls to help ensure compliance with activating cameras when required by policy,” GAO concluded in its report.

“Only CBP has automated controls, such as automatic camera activation technology. ICE does not have similar automated control activities in place to help ensure that personnel activate their cameras as required by policy or to reliably monitor whether repeated instances of failure to activate occur. This presents the risk of personnel not capturing footage of incidents when they are required to do so,” the GAO wrote, using an abbreviation for Customs and Border Protection.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) broadly agreed with GAO’s recommendations but rebuffed the suggestion of automated camera activation.

“DHS stated that, for ICE, automatic activation presents operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement. DHS also stated that these inadvertent or false activations could result in the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in First Amendment activities in areas where camera use is restricted,” the report states.

“However, DHS’s response did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective, or other controls that could help ensure compliance with activating cameras when required by policy.”

House Homeland Security Committee ranking member Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) said he would be introducing legislation to require automatic body camera activation.

“ICE — which has shown time and again it thinks it is immune to accountability — is unwilling to implement automatic activation for its cameras, increasing the risk of missing critical recordings, just like what happened when Wilber Garces Perez was shot by an ICE agent in Austin last month. This is completely unacceptable and I will be introducing legislation in the coming days to close this gap and ensure all DHS body-worn cameras have the recommended automatic activation,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Judge extends block on taxpayer-funded Trump ads until after midterms
articles.summary: A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on the Trump administration’s controversial ad campaign featuring President Trump until after the midterms. A temporary restraining order issued Sunday, which required the administration to stop airing the commercials and cancel any remaining ad placements, is now in effect until Nov. 8, U.S. District Judge Jennifer…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on the Trump administration’s controversial ad campaign featuring President Trump until after the midterms.

A temporary restraining order issued Sunday, which required the administration to stop airing the commercials and cancel any remaining ad placements, is now in effect until Nov. 8, U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon said in court filings .

The nearly $20 million ad campaign , which included at least five commercials promoting Trump and his policies, is being challenged by several groups as an illegal misuse of taxpayer funds.

The ads, paid for through money earmarked for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, have also been criticized as “political propaganda.” One 30 second spot features the president’s voice denouncing communism, socialism and Marxism and is set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN, who says the White House did not obtain his permission to use the music.

Each ad included a disclaimer tag stating it was “paid for by the U.S. government.”

When reached for comment Thursday, the White House pointed to a recent Truth Social post in which Trump called the ads a “rather standard thing to do” but pledged to pay for them himself or by using outside groups.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” the president wrote. “Although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

The White House has also claimed that the ads are no different from public service announcements used by prior administrations to highlight a president’s policies and vision for the country.

The Justice Department previously argued that the lawsuit was moot because the ads were slated to stop airing on Sunday night anyway. The judge, however, rejected that argument.

The challengers complained to the judge on Monday that the spots had continued to air hours after the initial halt was ordered on Sunday morning.

Justice Department lawyers apologized in court filings the next day, saying some federal employees did not see the order until that Monday morning, which delayed the cancellation of the already purchased ad time.

The Democratic National Committee is also suing over the ads , with a hearing slated for Thursday morning before a federal judge in the nation’s capital.

articles.summary: Democrats lead by 3 points on a generic ballot against Republicans with the midterms less than three weeks out, according to a new poll. The AARP poll, released Thursday, found 49 percent of respondents backed Democrats and 46 percent backed Republicans, while 5 percent were unsure about their choice of party. The slight lead for…
articles.body:
Democrats lead by 3 points on a generic ballot against Republicans with the midterms less than three weeks out, according to a new poll.

The AARP poll, released Thursday, found 49 percent of respondents backed Democrats and 46 percent backed Republicans, while 5 percent were unsure about their choice of party.

The slight lead for Democrats comes amid rocky political territory for the GOP. The party is facing down issues like the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living.

The poll surveyed 1,368 likely voters within congressional districts that the nonpartisan election handicapper labeled as toss-ups or leaning Republican or Democrat at the time, from Oct. 1-5. The margin of sampling error was 2.7 percentage points.

In the poll, Trump’s approval rating among respondents was 42 percent, with his disapproval at 56 percent.

Fox News earlier this week predicted Democrats will retake the House in this year’s midterms, the first time the outlet has predicted a win of either chamber of Congress by Democrats in this election cycle.

“Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the GOP this year,” Fox News contributor Rémy Numa said while discussing his latest power rankings, which were released Tuesday.

articles.title: Harris calls out Biden administration over Israel’s actions in Gaza war
articles.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Wednesday said the Biden administration should have responded sooner to the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” in the Gaza war. Harris was speaking at the Asan Memorial Lecture in Seoul, South Korea, where she said the U.S. had “fallen short” on its “moral obligation to human rights and international law,”…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Wednesday said the Biden administration should have responded sooner to the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” in the Gaza war.

Harris was speaking at the Asan Memorial Lecture in Seoul, South Korea, where she said the U.S. had “fallen short” on its “moral obligation to human rights and international law,” Israeli news outlet Haaretz reported .

“Most recently, the failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza, both under the current administration, which offers Netanyahu a blank check, and our administration before, where we should have acted sooner and more forcefully,” she said, referring to both the Biden and Trump administrations.

The Republican Jewish Coalition slammed Harris for the remark, calling it “unsurprising” on the social platform X .

The remarks are in stark contrast with the uniform approach that former President Biden’s administration held in response to the war in Gaza.

The administration’s handling of the conflict became a defining issue during the 2024 presidential election, in which Harris lost to President Trump. The Institute for Middle East Understanding and YouGov conducted a poll that found 29 percent of Americans who voted for Biden in 2020 did not vote for Harris in 2024 because of the former president’s support of Israel’s war in Gaza.

Israel launched the war following the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which left 1,200 dead. The ensuing war in Gaza killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is controlled by Hamas.

Biden said in April 2024 that U.S. support for Israel was “ironclad,” though he later voiced frustration with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his war tactics and civilian deaths in the territory. The former president’s support for Netanyahu and his government did not falter despite Biden’s criticism of the prime minister for “hurting Israel more than helping” with his handling of the war.

Biden and Harris faced massive demonstrations from pro-Palestinian protesters calling on the U.S. to stop sending arms to Israel, accusing the administration of authorizing a genocide in the Middle East. Human rights groups and United Nations-commissioned experts have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, a claim that Netanyahu has denied.

“Here’s the simple truth. Israel didn’t commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide,” Netanyahu said before the United Nations General Assembly last month , calling the accusation the “greatest lie of the century.”

President Trump announced the first phase of a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, following this with the creation of the Gaza Board of Peace in January to oversee the territory’s reconstruction.

articles.title: Trump cancels Hegseth’s planned livestream for Nidal Hasan execution
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday said he was canceling the livestream of the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army major who killed 13 people in the 2009 attack on Fort Hood. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said the execution would be livestreamed, a decision that had come under substantial criticism, including from GOP…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday said he was canceling the livestream of the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army major who killed 13 people in the 2009 attack on Fort Hood.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said the execution would be livestreamed, a decision that had come under substantial criticism, including from GOP senators who said it would bring the U.S. to the level of terrorist groups who broadcast executions.

Trump in his statement said he had heard that criticism, and he said that while Hasan deserved to be executed, it would not be livestreamed. He also argued the livestream might have deterred terrorists.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!”

Hasan killed 13 people and injured 32 others when he opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, in November 2009.

Hegseth announced plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution earlier this month, but even inside the administration, the decision seemed to have caused some discomfort.

Vice President Vance, for example, said Hasan deserved to die but that he would not be watching a livestream of the execution.

Several Republican members of the House and Senate pushed back at Hegseth’s decision, arguing the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families and that the livestream of the execution is an act only dictatorships perform.

“A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said last week, adding the planned livestream “risks feeding that appetite.”

“The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity,” Curtis said. “Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”

Hegseth announced the decision during an interview with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec, stating people need to comprehend the consequences for the act carried out by Hasan.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” the defense secretary said during the interview.

Over the weekend, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the decision to livestream the military execution, but emphasized that no one has to watch it.

“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

“I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” he added.

“I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies,” Mullin said.

Hasan opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center in November 2009 where he killed 13 people and injured 32 others in what was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

An American-born Muslim, Hasan was heard screaming “Allahu akbar” during the attack at the base, which ended when he was shot four times, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.

“Nidal Malik Hasan, a former U.S. Army Major turned traitor, is a very bad and evil man, who killed 13 people, including a pregnant soldier, who died, along with her unborn son, and injured, very seriously, 32 more innocent people. Barack Hussein Obama’s Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) intercepted electronic communications between Hasan and the radical Yemeni-American cleric, Anwar al-Awlaki. When reviewed by his FBI terrorism task force, investigators concluded that Hasan’s emails were not a threat. This assessment of the Obama Administration’s actions was later considered to be a key intelligence failure. With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

articles.title: House Democrats plan for next Congress
articles.summary: Some House Democrats are planning to reclaim legislative powers and address executive overreach through various legislative and oversight measures if they win back the majority in January.
articles.body:
While most House members were out this month rallying their supporters and beating the bushes for sufficient campaign funds to win reelection, a few Democrats were quietly working behind the scenes to plan for their possible takeover of the chamber next January.

At first glance, the Democrats’ preparations might seem an attempt to mimic minority House Republicans’ 1994 campaign platform, “ The Contract with America .” Under the tutelage of then-House Whip Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), who went on to become Speaker the following January, the GOP laid out its plans for taking control of the House in the 104th Congress (1995-96).

“The Contract with America” included ten major policy measures Republicans pledged to pass in their first 100-days in the majority, including welfare reform, anti-crime legislation and a presidential line-item veto. It also included a raft of internal House procedural reforms they promised to adopt on the opening day of the new Congress, such as term limits on committee chairmen and abolishing proxy voting.

What the Democrats are doing today is markedly different from the 1994 “Contract” scenario. For one thing, all House Republicans finalized and signed their Contract in September, well before the midterm elections and promised if they did not carry-out all their promises they should be thrown out of office at the next election. So far, Democrats have yet to coalesce around a common set of principles, let alone specific legislative details. Their move has been reactive rather than proactive — a pudding without a theme.

Secondly, the Democrats’ efforts are focused more on passing legislation that will seal loopholes in the law that President Trump has exploited to circumvent Congress and the courts. To date this belated pushback looks like an attempt to close the barn door after the horses have escaped; or, perhaps more accurately, to reconstruct a more durable barn, then rounding up the runaways and returning them to more secure stalls.

A leading proponent of this approach is Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, and its likely chairman if Democrats win back the majority. Relying on the same rebuilding analogy, Raskin said recently , “We have a massive reconstruction task ahead of us. Fortunately, reconstruction has a great history in our country.”

Raskin has been leading the charge to reclaim the powers of Congress, not only by closing the barn door to future presidential encroachments on Congress’s prerogatives, but by codifying that reclamation. He has already drafted bills to bar the president from accepting payments from foreign governments without congressional consent, and requiring congressional review before entering into any monetary settlements with his own government, such as the now defunct $1.8 billion victimization fund to reimburse those who claim to have been persecuted and prosecuted by government for their political views.

Other Democratic members have given top priority to limiting presidential powers to unilaterally declare emergencies, as President Trump did in imposing tariffs on foreign nations, implementing questionable deportations, and deploying National Guard troops and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest illegal criminal immigrants.

While some Democrats are already talking about using the impeachment power against the president (for a third time), others, like former President Barack Obama; former House member, ambassador to Japan and Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel; and political strategist James Carville, are warning against going down that dead-end road again and reviving rancorous hostilities.

Democrats are more focused for now on performing emergency triage to stop the bleeding of the First Branch and restoring the soundness of its original powers and responsibilities under the Constitution. Their instruments of choice will be their existing investigative and oversight powers to shine a light on previous excessive wrongdoing and rooting out executive mismanagement, abuses of power, and corruption, some of which could lead to criminal indictments.

Any immediate attempts at fully pursuing legislative fixes over the next two years will likely face vetoes by President Trump. It is unlikely that Democrats will gain sufficient seats next month to produce a two-thirds vote in both houses to override those vetoes. Meantime, support remains high in both chambers for ethics reforms to push back on rampant corruption in both branches.

This year may not be a 1994-styled congressional reform revolution, with substantive policy themes and glitzy procedural gimmicks. It nevertheless could produce some shift in powers from the executive branch back to the legislative. To spur turnout, the president has repeatedly urged his supporters to “pretend I am on the ballot.” In a spirit of faux bipartisanship, Democrats are gleefully embracing this call to play “let’s pretend.”

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2018).

articles.title: Multiple states report suspicious packages with white powder at election offices
articles.summary: Election officials in three states have reported suspicious packages were sent to their offices in the past week, only a few weeks out from the midterm elections. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said Wednesday that U.S. Postal Service investigators blocked the delivery of a letter containing a “powdery white substance” to his office. The…
articles.body:
Election officials in three states have reported suspicious packages were sent to their offices in the past week, only a few weeks out from the midterm elections .

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said Wednesday that U.S. Postal Service investigators blocked the delivery of a letter containing a “powdery white substance” to his office. The secretary said the FBI was handling this investigation.

“Election officials should never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties, and there is no place in a peaceful democracy for violence, threats or acts of intimidation,” he said in a statement shared on social media.

“We have a duty to the citizens of Ohio to deliver secure and accessible elections, and these kinds of cowardly threats will not deter us from that mission,” LaRose continued.

In Oklahoma, Paul Ziriax, the secretary of the state’s election board, said in a statement that its office was evacuated on Tuesday after it received an envelope that contained “suspicious white powder.”

Ziriax thanked the response from state troopers and other Oklahoma law enforcement agencies to this incident and said no one was injured.

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections,” he said. “Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections.”

Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry announced in a Tuesday afternoon social media post that her office’s Baton Rouge building had been evacuated after an elections employee opened a package and discovered a “white powder.”

In an update later that evening, she said law enforcement had found “no evidence of harmful substances” after running tests on the substance and that her office would continue to review the incident to identify safety improvement areas.

The FBI confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner, that the agency and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service were investigating the packages.

“We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” an FBI spokesperson said in a Thursday statement. “This FBI will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”

Ahead of the 2024 presidential election, election officials in several states reported receiving packages that contained white powder.

The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said they were “deeply concerned” about these new reports in a joint statement released on Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” the organizations said. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”

articles.title: 80 percent oppose Hegseth’s push to livestream Fort Hood shooter execution: Survey
articles.summary: Most Americans are against the livestreaming of the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, according to a new poll. In the ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, 80 percent of respondents were against former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan’s execution being “live streamed online for the American public to watch.” Eighteen percent were for livestreaming the execution…
articles.body:
Most Americans are against the livestreaming of the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, according to a new poll .

In the ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, 80 percent of respondents were against former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan’s execution being “live streamed online for the American public to watch.” Eighteen percent were for livestreaming the execution and 2 percent did not answer the question.

The survey arrived hours before President Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Thursday that Hasan “will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”

“That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose,” the president added.

Last Thursday , Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad execution of Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood shooter, would be publicly viewable. Hasan is a former Army psychiatrist who in 2009 opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, leaving 13 dead.

Hasan is set to be executed on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at Fort Hood, the U.S. Army has said. It would be the first U.S. military execution in more than six decades and the first by firing squad since World War II.

“Of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood. We’re going to do it on a Thursday, we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad,” Hegseth told Real America’s Voice last week.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he added.

The poll found 53 percent of respondents backed the firing squad execution of Hasan, while 42 percent were against it and 6 percent did not respond to the question.

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll took place from Oct. 9 to 13, featuring 2,545 people and plus or minus 2 percentage points as its margin of error.

articles.body:
President Trump dismissed reporting that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s job is in jeopardy Thursday.

The White House issued a response from the president himself to Politico after the outlet reported that Trump has received negative feedback about Wiles from allies after soliciting their opinions about his chief of staff.

“TOTAL FAKE NEWS Politico doesn’t care about facts, integrity, or honest journalism — it’s why I kicked them out of the White House!” Trump said in a statement to the outlet. “Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that. She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Wiles is considered one of Trump’s most trusted advisers and confidants. She has played a major role in shaping his second administration and in securing his 2024 presidential victory as co-campaign manager.

Trump has also publicly praised Wiles on numerous occasions. After Wiles announced that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, Trump referred to her as “an amazing person” and “an amazing fighter.” Wiles announced last month that she was cancer free .

Politico’s reporting comes weeks after news surfaced that Trump political advisers James Blair and Chris LaCivita, who served as Wiles’s co-campaign manager in 2024, were paid to travel to the Balkans to advise a pro-Russian political party ahead of an election there.

Trump said in a Truth Social post that he was not aware the two had taken the trip and that he would fire them if any wrongdoing took place.

articles.title: The myth of the ‘humane’ firing squad execution
articles.summary: The firing squad was not chosen on evidence that it produces a death free of cruelty. It was written in by prisoners who had to fill in a blank with nothing else left to write.
articles.body:
President Trump, who under military law must approve any death sentence a court-martial imposes, has ordered that former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan be executed by firing squad.

Hasan was convicted in 2013 of the Nov. 5, 2009, mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. The military had adopted lethal injection as its method of execution; the switch to shooting came without explanation. The U.S. military last used a firing squad in 1945 . Hasan, paralyzed from the waist down after being shot during the attack, will likely be seated when he is shot.

The choice will be defended as clean and quick. That reputation is unearned. The firing squad’s reputation as a cruelty-free method was not built on evidence — it was built by condemned prisoners whom the courts forced to name a less cruel way to die. I know, because I testify as a medical expert in those cases.

When it comes to cruel execution methods, Hasan’s case inverts the discourse. Civilian prisoners proposed the firing squad because the law left them no other option. When asked recently why the firing squad, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s reply was simply: “No-brainer.” Historically, the firing squad was considered an honorable death for a soldier, while alternative execution methods like hanging were disgraceful criminal punishments. It is uncertain if Hasan considers his impending execution an opportunity to show bravery and exhibit honor. Judged by Hegseth’s rhetoric, an honorable, cruelty-free death for Hasan does not appear to be the goal. The violence is the message.

The Constitution’s Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishment, and that includes the way the state kills. But in capital punishment, the law has shifted the duty to prove and disprove cruelty in punishment from the state to the prisoner. In Glossip v. Gross (2015), the Supreme Court held that a prisoner who challenges a method of execution as cruel must also identify a known and available alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain. In Bucklew v. Precythe (2019) , the court reaffirmed that rule. The state does not have to prove its method is not cruel; the prisoner has to propose a better way to be killed.

Some states go further and let prisoners choose a method outright. The Uniform Code of Military Justice offers no comparable path. Hasan has no way to bring a method claim at all.

I saw firsthand what that rule does as an expert witness in Bucklew. Russell Bucklew, on Missouri’s death row, had cavernous hemangiomas : expanding, blood-filled tumors in his throat that were slowly closing his airway. I examined him while he was on death row in Missouri. He could not lie flat. I warned that lethal injection could cause him to choke on his own blood, and that he could vomit blood in front of witnesses. That prospect was enough to win him a stay and further proceedings.

Bucklew then had to name an alternative means of execution. He proposed nitrogen gas, and the court asked me whether it would be less cruel. As a physician practicing ethically, I cannot recommend a way to kill a person, and the American Medical Association filed an amicus brief supporting that position. No matter. The court found that my refusal left a hole in Bucklew’s argument. Nitrogen gas was also not yet available; in effect, the court required Bucklew to build his own gas chamber.

Meanwhile, he needed an urgent tracheostomy to keep from choking to death. With the tracheostomy tube in place, he could lie flat, and the choking risk at the center of his claim lost its force. Missouri executed him in 2019.

If not lethal injection and not nitrogen gas, what is left? In 2017, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in a dissent that the firing squad might be more reliable than lethal injection. Since then, prisoners have increasingly named it in their complaints, and five U.S. states now authorize it: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. When a prisoner offers the firing squad, he is satisfying a legal requirement, not vouching for its mercy. No real data shows the method is not cruel, and no prospective study supports any method of execution.

The evidence that does exist is not reassuring. In April 2025, South Carolina executed Mikal Mahdi by firing squad. An autopsy commissioned by his defense team and reported by independent pathologist Dr. Jonathan Arden concluded that the shots struck low or missed the heart entirely . Bullets pierced the liver, pancreas and lower lung. Mahdi did not die immediately. Witnesses heard him groan after he was shot.

The rule is still producing the same result. On Sept. 30, 2026, Tennessee tried and failed to execute Christa Pike with pentobarbital. I was an expert medical witness for Pike. In a written report and then on the stand, I warned that her history of difficult IV access, combined with a condition that made her blood prone to clotting , meant lethal injection could be protracted and painful, and could fail. The court set my concerns aside, and Tennessee proceeded.

During the procedure, her IVs infiltrated, leaking into tissues under the skin, causing significant burning and blistering. The pentobarbital never made it to her brain in sufficient quantity to kill her. She was transferred to intensive care at a Nashville hospital and is now back in her Tennessee prison undergoing further recovery.

For Pike, challenging the method was not enough. She, too, had to name a feasible, readily available method that would kill her without cruelty. Her lawyers first resisted on religious grounds. Pike is Buddhist , and her faith’s first precept forbids killing or harming any living thing, oneself included; naming the means of her own death would make her a participant in it.

Military and civilian systems alike are bound by the ban on cruel punishment. Civilian courts do not make the state prove its method is not cruel; they make the prisoner name one that is less so. Hasan does not even get that. When he faces the firing squad, seated, the method’s reputation should be understood for what it is. The firing squad was not chosen on evidence that it produces a death free of cruelty. It was written in by prisoners who had to fill in a blank with nothing else left to write.

Joel Zivot, MD, is a professor of anesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta. He was retained as a medical expert by Christa Pike’s defense team prior to her attempted execution.

articles.title: Early winter weather predictions released by NOAA
articles.summary: Brown Thanksgiving? Warm Christmas? It’s possible, depending on where you live.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Warmer and dry or about-normal and wet – that’s the way late fall and early winter are expected to be divided in the U.S., according to the latest outlook.

As it did in September , the latest seasonal forecast from NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center shows a country divided.

The forecast, released Thursday, shows the kind of broad weather patterns each state can expect through the last two months of 2026 and the first of 2027, falling roughly in line with what is expected from the “historic” El Niño we’re facing .

States in the northern half of the country – from the Pacific Northwest, along the Canadian border, through the Midwest, into the Ohio Valley eastward, and north to New England – have the highest probability of seeing above-average warmth between November and January.

An expanding group of states – including all or parts of Louisiana, Arkansas, Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, Idaho, and California – are not leaning above-average this fall. That doesn’t mean it will be cold, necessarily; it just means the forecast is less clear, giving the states an equal chance of seeing a warm, cool, or normal winter season.

The precipitation outlook is flipped, however.

Many of the same states expected to trend warmer are also more likely to be dry. A large, W-shaped swath to the south – from California to Florida and north to New England, as well as a group in the central Plains – are leaning toward above-average rain. Florida and its nearby neighbors from the Gulf to the East Coast, as well as southern California and Arizona, have the highest probability.

Meanwhile, portions of Montana, Idaho, Washington, Wyoming, North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Alaska have the highest probability of a dry winter.

These forecasts are roughly what is expected during a typical El Niño year, with the dividing line across the country shifting depending on the position of the jet stream.

Earlier this month, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said in its latest update that El Niño “strengthened further last month,” with “a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely” from January through March.

“Chances remain high for a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950,” the latest guidance from the CPC explained . “With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed.”

articles.title: Warren calls Treasury Department fine of Bank of America a ‘slap-on-the-wrist’
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) on Wednesday blasted the Treasury Department’s $1.2 billion fine of Bank of America as “a slap-on-the-wrist fine.” Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that Bank of America “failed to implement an effective anti-money laundering program for years.” In announcing the penalty, the Treasury…
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) on Wednesday blasted the Treasury Department’s $1.2 billion fine of Bank of America as “a slap-on-the-wrist fine.”

Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that Bank of America “failed to implement an effective anti-money laundering program for years.”

In announcing the penalty, the Treasury Department said the country’s second-largest bank violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

The financial institution failed to “mitigate and report priority national security risks” to regulators, the department said in the press release . Those risks included “suspicious transactions” indicative of activity by Chinese money laundering networks and southwest border cartels, the department noted.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the penalty — the third-largest in his department’s history — showed that “even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.”

But Warren cast the penalty in a different light, noting the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) warned Bank of America in 2024 to address its “deficient” money-laundering compliance program.

“The Biden Administration failed to hold Bank of America accountable in 2024, and now, the Trump Administration is letting Bank of America off the hook with a slap-on-the-wrist fine that represents a small fraction of the $30 billion in profits the bank made last year alone,” the Massachusetts Democrat added.

“Real accountability would mean imposing an asset cap and restrictions on shareholder dividends and stock buybacks and conducting a criminal investigation into the apparent violation of our anti-money laundering laws,” she continued, before calling on Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan to testify to Congress.

A spokesperson for Bank of America said the company “worked with regulators” to reach the penalty resolutions after the OCC issued its 2024 order and the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network conducted its probe.

“We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year,” the spokesperson added.

The institution on Wednesday reported $6.9 billion in net income during the third quarter, a total that accounted for the Treasury Department’s $1.2 billion penalty.

Bank of America also reported $30 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 3 percent from the third quarter of 2025 but down 5 percent from the second quarter of this year.

The bank’s stock rebounded Wednesday, closing at $51.39 per share after sinking below its opening mark of $49.83 during trading. The company’s stock was up Thursday, trading at above $51.40 per share as of the late morning.

Warren is in line to chair the Senate Banking panel if Democrats win control of the upper chamber in the midterms, now less than three weeks away.

The progressive senator added Wednesday that large banks “should be subject to structural punishments” and executives “should be held personally accountable when they break the law.”

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who is running for reelection, said Wednesday that Republicans in Georgia “do not want” President Trump to campaign for them in the Peach State.

“I know for a fact, because I talked to some of the Republican officeholders, folks here in Georgia, Georgia Republicans do not want the president to come,” Ossoff told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes on “All In.”

“My Trump puppet opponent, the bigot Congressman Mike Collins, is probably the only Republican in Georgia who actually wants Donald Trump to come,” he added.

“The president’s deeply unpopular here. The war is unpopular. The tariffs are unpopular. The healthcare cuts and doubled health insurance premiums are deeply unpopular.”

However, Ossoff also added that, “if the president wants to come to Georgia right now, that’s OK with me.”

Trump is set to rally in Dalton, Ga., on Friday , amid rocky political territory for the president and his party. As the midterm elections near, the GOP is dealing with issues including the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.7 percent on Thursday morning, with his disapproval rating at 59.4 percent .

The war in Iran has driven up energy prices in the U.S., with the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, closed amid the fighting. According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.33 on Thursday morning, up from about $3.07 last year at the same time.
