articles.title: Former Cruz spokesperson: ‘It’s going to be a bad night’ for Republicans in midterms
articles.summary: GOP political operative Rick Tyler said Wednesday the Republican Party is facing “a lot of problems” headed into the November elections, as the GOP vies to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. During an appearance on “CNN News Central,” the former spokesperson for Sen. Ted Cruz’s (R) 2016 presidential campaign cited tight midterm races…
articles.body:
GOP political operative Rick Tyler said Wednesday the Republican Party is facing “a lot of problems” headed into the November elections, as the GOP vies to maintain control of both chambers of Congress.

During an appearance on “CNN News Central,” the former spokesperson for Sen. Ted Cruz’s (R) 2016 presidential campaign cited tight midterm races in Alaska, Michigan, Iowa and Ohio.

“It’s going to be a bad night for Republicans,” Tyler said, referring to Election Day. “It just is. How bad? We don’t know.”

While Tyler acknowledged affordability concerns were “the main issue” for voters this election cycle, he warned against reading these election results as a referendum on President Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war.

“That’s not what it is; it is just a rejection of the status quo,” he said. “And that’s all it is, and that’s what the Democrats ought to read into it. They won’t — they’ll overreach.”

The Republican operative also pointed to the enthusiasm gap between each party’s voter base. In an AP-NORC poll released Thursday, 76 percent of registered Democratic voters and 63 percent of registered Republican voters said voting this November was “extremely important” to them.

“If you look at who’s excited to vote and who’s not excited to vote, it’s clear that the Democrats have a huge advantage in being excited to go out and vote because they feel like they can win the House,” Tyler said. “I think they most certainly will, and they could win the Senate. And that’s what remains to be seen.”

articles.title: Enough is enough. It’s time for America to end executions.
articles.summary: An opinion piece by Yasmin Cader argues for the abolition of the death penalty following several botched executions and the Pentagon’s announcement of plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan.
articles.body:
Over the past two weeks, America has been forced to confront the stark reality of our continued use of the death penalty. Following a botched execution in Tennessee, the Trump administration announced plans to turn an execution into a grim spectacle broadcast for the world to watch, only to reverse course after widespread backlash . These atrocities expose the cruelty of a fundamentally flawed practice that has repeatedly proven inhumane and error prone. It’s time we stop asking how to make executions more palatable and start asking why we continue to carry them out at all.

On Oct. 8, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the Pentagon planned to livestream the execution by firing squad of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood. The planned execution would mark a somber national milestone: the first military execution in the United States in more than six decades. Broadcasting it would have placed the United States in the shameful company of authoritarian governments that use public executions to display state power and intimidate their populations. The proposal drew widespread criticism, including from former military officials, the pope, and members of the administration’s own party. Thursday, President Trump announced that the execution would no longer be livestreamed, though it remains scheduled to proceed by firing squad.

Eight days before Hegseth’s announcement, Tennessee failed to execute Christa Pike. She survived two doses of lethal injection drugs during the execution attempt that left her hospitalized in critical condition.

We have become so committed to preserving the death penalty that evidence of its cruelty becomes another problem to solve so that executions can continue. A botched execution prompts a search for better procedures. A proposed public execution prompts demands to keep the killing out of sights. Each controversy becomes a debate about how to make the punishment acceptable. These events should instead force us to confront what we are working so hard to preserve — and why.

Less than five months before its attempt to execute Pike, Tennessee subjected Tony Carruthers to a torturous execution attempt. On May 21, the state spent more than 90 minutes trying to establish an IV line in Carruthers’s arms, hands, feet, and chest, puncturing his body more than a dozen times while he groaned in pain. After nearly 90 minutes, the state abandoned its attempt. He was left bloodied and traumatized before being returned to his cell, where the Tennessee Department of Correction gave him ibuprofen for his pain.

Carruthers’s and Pike’s experiences exposed the violence that lethal injection was designed to conceal. The medical setting and the false promise of a peaceful death was supposed to make state-sanctioned killing look like a clinical procedure. But changing the appearance of an execution does not change the underlying reality.

For decades, death penalty states, the federal government, and military persist in wielding the power of the state to kill people, finding new methods and reviving old ways to kill. The results of their grim experimentation show us there is no way to guarantee a peaceful, cruelty-free execution.

In 2024, Kenneth Smith writhed and gasped for minutes during Alabama’s first execution by nitrogen hypoxia, despite officials’ assurances that the experimental method would be “painless and quick.” In 2025, a South Carolina firing squad shot Mikal Mahdi in a way that left him “alive and reacting longer than was intended or expected” after they shot him. That same year, Byron Black groaned and told his spiritual advisor he was in pain as Tennessee executed him by lethal injection. His autopsy later revealed fluid buildup in his lungs, a condition experts say can feel like drowning.

Our commitment to preserving executions has even produced a constitutional absurdity. Under the Supreme Court’s rules, a person challenging an execution method as unconstitutionally painful must identify a feasible, readily implemented alternative that would significantly reduce the risk of severe pain. To invoke the Constitution’s protection against cruelty, they must help identify another way for the state to kill them. Their claim to constitutional protection becomes a dispute over how their execution should proceed.

The Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment rests on respect for human dignity. That principle should guide our judgment of the punishment itself. We should be asking what this record of suffering and the prospect of televised and celebrated state-sanctioned killing tells us about the death penalty, and how much cruelty were are prepared to accept to keep it.

Executions behind closed doors shield the public from the prolonged, painful deaths including those officially deemed successful. But the people who witness them — including victims’ families, legal teams, media witnesses, and corrections officers — are not shielded from the trauma. Secrecy does not eliminate the suffering. It simply makes it easier for the rest of us to look away.

The backlash to the Pentagon’s proposed livestream offers an opportunity to break this pattern. For those who support executions but recoiled at the prospect of a spectacle, the challenge is to carry that scrutiny beyond the cameras and into the punishment itself.

We should stop treating each new horror as a problem to work around and recognize it for what it is — a practice we cannot justifiably repair. Our constitutional commitment to human dignity demands that we end the death penalty.

Yasmin Cader is deputy executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union.

articles.title: Perceptions of multiple Cabinet departments decline: Gallup
articles.summary: Fewer Americans rated the performance of some Cabinet departments as “excellent” or “good” compared with last year, according to a survey released Thursday. The result is from Gallup’s annual governance poll, which asks Americans to rate the job performance of five federal Cabinet departments and 12 government agencies. The annual rating for four Cabinet departments…
articles.body:
Fewer Americans rated the performance of some Cabinet departments as “excellent” or “good” compared with last year, according to a survey released Thursday.

The result is from Gallup’s annual governance poll , which asks Americans to rate the job performance of five federal Cabinet departments and 12 government agencies. The annual rating for four Cabinet departments was worse than what they were a year ago.

“Ratings of the State, Justice and Defense Departments are now the lowest Gallup has measured for each in readings dating back to 2021 or 2022,” the Gallup report said.

Dropping 8 percentage points, 40 percent of Americans favorably rated the performance of the Department of Defense. For the Department of State, the number dropped from 34 percent to 27 percent. About 27 percent of those polled rated the Justice Department’s performance favorably, compared with 31 percent in 2025.

Last year, 42 percent rated the Department of Homeland Security favorably, and the number has now come down to 36 percent, the poll showed.

“After illegal border crossings plummeted in late 2024 and 2025, the department’s job rating improved to 42% last year,” the Gallup report said. “Some recent immigration enforcement encounters have turned deadly, likely contributing to this year’s lower rating.”

The survey showed the Justice Department had the highest percentage of negative ratings, with about 48 percent saying “it is doing a poor job.” This is 21 percentage points higher than its positive rating.

Meanwhile, the Department of Veterans Affairs saw an improvement in ratings as compared with last year. The number rose from 25 percent last year to 31 percent this year.

The Gallup report said Republicans, including Republican-leaning independents, are responsible for more positive ratings than Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents toward the Cabinet departments.

“No more than 24% of Democrats rate any of the Cabinets positively, with a low of 11% for the Justice Department,” the report said.

The U.S. Postal Service and NASA, out of the 12 government agencies included in the survey, showed higher positive ratings while the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention received the lowest good ratings.

The Gallup poll was conducted Sept. 1-17 and had a margin of error of 4 percentage points.

“His ability to navigate the complex landscape of our economy, tackle the national debt with a steady hand, and work towards solutions that bridge divides is especially critical in today’s challenging political climate,” Bolduc continued.

The Democratic nominee welcomed Bolduc’s endorsement in a social media post on Friday morning.

“We’re building a growing coalition of Republicans, Democrats, and independents who are willing to put country before party and work toward a better future,” Pappas said. “Grateful to everyone who’s joining this team.”

Pappas has maintained his lead in the race to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D). In a New Hampshire Institute of Politics poll released Tuesday, the Democrat had a 7-point advantage among likely voters in the state. A September survey from The New York Times and Siena University showed the Democrat ahead by 5 points in the midterm contest.

The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating of the race from a “toss-up” to leaning in favor of Democrats earlier this month following positive polling numbers for Pappas.

articles.title: Cleft lip and palate and other craniofacial surgery for kids isn’t cosmetic, it’s lifesaving
articles.summary: The Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act aims to prevent insurance companies from wrongfully denying medically necessary surgeries for children and adults born with congenital facial conditions.
articles.body:
It should be fundamentally irrational to all Americans that an insurer can deem a surgery that is required for a child to eat, breathe or speak as “cosmetic.” But this has been happening for years, and we have a solution in Congress. The Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act (ELSA) will guarantee that children and adults born with congenital facial conditions such as cleft lip or cleft palate receive the medically necessary care they deserve without wrongful insurance denials, often costing families tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket.

Despite existing state laws such as “ Wendolyn’s Law” in Arkansas , patients still face delays and denials for vital treatments, leaving families to foot the bill — insurance loopholes that bankrupt households who choose to help their child over all else.

About 4 percent of U.S. children are born with congenital anomalies impacting essential functions like swallowing, chewing, breathing, and hearing, yet health insurance denials continue despite state mandates. Roughly 1 in 1,000 babies born in the U.S. has a cleft lip and/or cleft palate. While congenital heart defects are more common, parents of a child with a craniofacial condition frequently face denials of coverage, including retroactively denying cases after a procedure has been completed. Can we imagine a world in which insurance companies denied patients the right to have pediatric heart surgery as “not medically necessary”?

ELSA ensures coverage for medically necessary treatments, not cosmetic procedures. When a child born with a cleft palate requires surgery to restore normal jaw function so they may chew and swallow correctly for the rest of their life, this is not cosmetic or elective; it is necessary. But right now, a health insurance company might declare the procedure should be covered by dental insurance and bounce it, only for a dental insurance company to push it back to medical — only to be denied.

In fact, even when the leading global experts at Approved Cleft and Craniofacial Teams write letters specifying why a procedure is medically necessary for proper function, insurance companies are still finding ways to deny a claim, many times with the claim review performed by family physicians and not by the experts who treat patients with craniofacial conditions.

Allowing a growing child or young adult to have a healthy, functioning facial structure is not something that should be up for debate because of insurance. Nonprofits receive letters asking for assistance from families around the country, in every state, from all walks of life and political affiliations. The stories we hear from mothers, fathers, grandparents, and patients are heartbreaking, and have been happening for years .

From families who have been denied insurance coverage of a child’s secondary bone graft surgery, so their child no longer has a hole in the roof of their mouth, to a story about an older child with a cleft lip who can’t breathe properly out of their nose and who is mocked in grade school — creating bullying and long-lasting emotional trauma — while a pediatric cleft surgeon could remedy the issue if the family could pay for it. These are medically necessary procedures, yet families can still get caught between medical and dental insurers and be left with enormous bills.

With wide bipartisan support and more than 70 professional societies and patient groups in support, including Sens. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) and Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) and Reps. Neal Dunn, M.D. (R-Fla.) and Kim Schrier, M.D. (D-Wash.), ELSA is not controversial; it is essential. Families go through repeated complex procedures, many of which must be done in sequential order. A child may have 16 procedures by the time they are 16 years old — none are cosmetic. Individuals who do not receive timely, continuous care for their congenital anomalies face long-term physical and psychological injuries.

It’s time for Congress to help these families and pass the Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act, protecting Americans from financial ruin and, more importantly, helping children who deserve to live happy, fulfilling, healthy lives.

Adam Levy is executive director of the American Cleft Palate Craniofacial Association, the premier scientific resource and interdisciplinary professional network for healthcare providers serving patients with cleft lip, cleft palate, and craniofacial differences.

It’s Thursday. As always, there is a lot to cover today. Let’s dive in.

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com or awalker@thehill.com .

President Trump on Thursday announced that the execution of Fort Hood shooter U.S. Army Major Nidal Hasan would no longer be livestreamed .

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The president said that victims’ immediate families would still be able to view the Dec. 3 firing squad execution in person, adding, “They deserve to witness JUSTICE!”

Not a fan: Polling released Thursday found that the decision to livestream the execution was unpopular among Americans .

An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found that 80 percent of respondents opposed the choice and only 18 percent approved.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced last week that the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people on the Texas Army post in 2009, would be public, prompting bipartisan backlash.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told Real America’s Voice last Thursday.

New polling from Fox News found Trump’s overall approval rating at its lowest ever across both terms, with Americans particularly frustrated with the economic matters.

The survey released Wednesday found that 36 percent of respondents approved the president’s job, while 64 percent disapproved.

Among key issues, Trump’s management of inflation was lowest, with only 22 percent approval compared to 36 percent in a Fox News survey done last summer.

Seventy percent of Americans were dissatisfied with the president’s overall handling of the economy and 69 percent disapproved of his tariff-related policies.

Trump scored highest on border security—where respondents were split 50-50 on his job.

The Fox News poll is the latest in a series of lackluster surveys and poses a potential bad omen for the GOP as the midterms quickly approach.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said she misinterpreted a question earlier this week about where she passed the bar exam to which she’d answered that she took the test after moving to China.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” Zacharia told The New York Times on a Wednesday phone call.

“That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” Zacharia added. “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.”

The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports, “The development comes as Zacharia’s legal credentials have come under intense scrutiny after the left-leaning newsletter Popular Information reported that Zacharia is not licensed to practice law in the U.S. or Washington, D.C.”

The watchdog group Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California state bar on Wednesday, accusing Zacharia of illegally inflating her legal credentials.

Thursday kicks off Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) two-day swing through Michigan with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Painting the town blue: The pair is stopping in redder parts of the state’s Upper Peninsula on Thursday that Trump won back in 2024. They hit Escanaba at noon, and are set to visit Iron Mountain at 2 p.m. and Marquette at 6:30 p.m.

On Friday, Ocasio-Cortez is venturing solo to a “Latinos for Abdul” rally in Detroit.

Is there more in Michigan for AOC?: This mini tour is a testing ground for the Democratic rep to see how her progressive messaging lands outside of New York.

The Hill’s Amie Parnes also wrote that a win for El-Sayed could strengthen the congresswoman’s potential bid for president in 2028.

“That will set the tone for the 2028 primary field and will do a lot to prove theories from all sides of the Democratic coalition,” according to Democratic strategist Joel Payne.

Vance is in Michigan, too: The VP will be the keynote speaker at a GOP rally this afternoon in Monroe, Mich.

A new AARP poll released Thursday found that Democrats lead Republicans by 3 points on a generic ballot against Republicans.

The poll found that 49 percent of respondents backed Democrats and 46 percent backed Republicans, while 5 percent were unsure about their choice of party.

The GOP has been facing backlash over the unpopular war in Iran, the rising price of diesel and gas, concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s slumping approval rating.

The federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) has escalated , according to The Associated Press , which reported Thursday that authorities seized her phone and issued many subpoenas, including to some of the Democrat’s family members.

Among those subpoenaed is Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor, and at least one additional relative, per The New York Times .

On Monday, Homeland Security Investigations sent agents to search Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence as part of a criminal investigation announced by White House border czar Tom Homan in September.

Trump and other Republicans have accused the Minnesota lawmaker of fraud and questioned her immigration status, claims Omar has repeatedly denied.

Election officials in the three states reported that suspicious packages were sent to their offices ahead of November’s midterms.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said on Wednesday that U.S. Postal Service investigators blocked the delivery of a letter containing a “powdery white substance” to his office. He added that the FBI is handling an investigation.

Oklahoma’s Secretary of the Election Board Paul Ziriax said in a statement that the state’s office was evacuated Tuesday after receiving an envelope with “suspicious white powder.”

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections,” he said. “Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections.”

And Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry’s Baton Rouge office was evacuated after an election employee opened a package and discovered a “white powder” on Tuesday.

She later said law enforcement found “no evidence of harmful substances” after running tests on the substance.

Deja vu?: Election officials in five states back in 2024 were sent suspicious packages. There were no reports that they contained hazardous material.

The packages also contained a powdery substance and were sent to Nebraska, Tennessee, Wyoming, Oklahoma and Iowa.

Trump dismissed reports that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is on thin ice. Politico had reported that she received negative feedback from his allies, but the president responded to the outlet with a statement that said, “TOTAL FAKE NEWS Politico doesn’t care about facts, integrity, or honest journalism — it’s why I kicked them out of the White House!”

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) subpoenaed both Anthropic and OpenAI on Wednesday in the newest development in the federal investigation into the AI model’s potential harms to consumers. The probe arrives following notable cases of cybersecurity breaches involving rogue AI agents.

articles.summary: Most voters want major change in Washington ahead of this year’s midterms, a new AP-NORC poll finds. That includes 97 percent of Democrats, 90 percent of independents and even…
articles.body:
Most voters want major change in Washington ahead of this year’s midterms, a new AP-NORC poll finds.

Overall, a combined 80 percent of registered voters say they want either “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in the way the country is run. That includes 97 percent of Democrats, 90 percent of independents and even a majority — 58 percent — of Republicans. Just 13 percent of Republicans said they wanted “complete and total upheaval,” however.

The new poll comes amid a midterm environment likely to be poor for Republicans. President Trump’s job approval in the AP-NORC survey is at just 36 percent, with 64 percent disapproving.

Because Republicans control the House and Senate, voters seeking major change may look to the main alternative: the Democrats. Registered voters surveyed in the AP-NORC poll preferred Democrats to control the House by a 9-point margin, and the Senate by an 8-point margin.

But in the survey, Democrats are barely more popular than the president, with just 4 in 10 having a favorable view of the Democratic Party.

The general anti-incumbent sentiment could explain mixed poll results in the Senate, which show both parties on weak footing in some usually reliable states.

In Kansas for example — a state Trump won by 16 points in 2024 — nonpartisan election data site Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, has Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in a close race with pastor Adam Hamilton (D). In DDHQ’s forecast, Marshall has a 65 percent chance to win reelection, but trails by 0.9 percent in the average of polls.

Democrats in Minnesota also find a closer than expected race. Former Vice President Harris won Minnesota by 4 points in 2024, but despite the Democratic lead nationally, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) leads former NFL reporter Michelle Tafoya (R) by just 3.7 points in DDHQ’s polling average.

Minnesota Democrats have been under fire for months after some Republicans, including Trump, blamed Gov. Tim Walz’s (D) administration for a healthcare fraud scheme in the state in which 15 people were indicted. Polls suggest that Flanagan, Walz’s lieutenant governor, could have taken a hit for the scandal.

DDHQ still gives Flanagan an 82 percent chance to win.

Voters in the AP-NORC survey also do not expect politics to improve, having little faith in either party or the direction of American politics.

Just 21 percent are very or somewhat optimistic about the future of the Democratic Party, and just 23 percent for the future of the Republican Party. For the state of politics in the U.S., just 10 percent say they are optimistic. Sixty-seven percent are somewhat or very pessimistic.

The AP-NORC survey was conducted Oct. 8-12 among 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters. The margin of error among adults is ±3.9 points, and ±4.2 points among the registered voters.

articles.body:
Six in 10 respondents to a recent Fox News survey said they were “extremely concerned” about government corruption ahead of November’s midterms, putting it ahead of inflation, healthcare and other issues.

Nearly 90 percent of 1,202 people polled said they were either extremely or “very concerned” about government corruption, ahead of “inflation and high prices” — at 85 percent, as their top area of concern.

A clear majority of respondents also were either extremely or very concerned about gas prices, at 83 percent, and healthcare, 80 percent.

Just 12 percent of those surveyed said they were “not very” or “not at all concerned” about government corruption.

Fox News’ pollsters conducted the survey from Oct. 9-12. It has a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.

Democrats have vowed to investigate President Trump and administration officials if they retake control of Congress, accusing them of corruption . Trump’s net worth has risen since retaking the White House in 2024, as he has benefitted from his family’s cryptocurrency ventures and his own stock trades — both of which liberal lawmakers have flagged as areas of concern.

Congress has also failed to pass legislation banning its members from trading stocks, despite clear public support for it.

Senate Democrats last month blocked a bill that GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts (Neb.) introduced to restrict lawmakers from buying new stocks of publicly traded companies.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said the Stop Insider Trading Act, which House lawmakers passed in July , was a “permission slip for corruption” and did not go far enough.

Pocketbook issues remain top of mind for voters, with midterm early voting underway in some states.

Nearly 6 in 10 respondents to the Fox News poll said the cost of living was the country’s top economic issue. More than half of respondents also said inflation was “not at all” under control.

Annual inflation, as measured by the consumer price index , has increased from 3 percent in January 2025 to 3.7 percent last month .

Gas prices remain above $4 per gallon amid the Iran war . A gallon of regular gas costs roughly $4.33 on average as of Thursday, according to AAA .

articles.title: Congress banned sending wild horses to slaughter. A loophole is undoing that promise.
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of lawmakers has called for a Government Accountability Office review of the Bureau of Land Management’s Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program to address significant gaps in post-sale oversight and prevent animals from entering the slaughter pipeline.
articles.body:
Washington can turn almost any subject into a partisan cage match. Wild horses are one of the rare exceptions. For decades, Congress has said federally protected mustangs should not be slaughtered. The promise is clear. What occurs after the government sells a mustang — that may ultimately become processed meat in a dinner abroad — is not.

While federal law does not categorically ban the slaughter of every horse or the export of domestic horses for slaughter, wild horses managed by the Bureau of Land Management have distinct protections. The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 says these animals should be protected from “capture, branding, harassment, or death.” Congress has also repeatedly barred the use of appropriated funds to destroy healthy wild horses or conduct sales that result in their processing into commercial products .

Then comes the catch. A 2004 amendment directs the Bureau of Land Management to sell certain animals that are older than 10 or have been offered unsuccessfully for adoption at least three times. Once the sale is complete, the animal is no longer legally considered a wild horse or burro. The Bureau of Land Management acknowledges that it does not track animals after sale because they have left its jurisdiction. Federal protection ends at the point when oversight may matter most.

In 2025, the Bureau of Land Management sold approximately 3,700 wild horses, more than twice the previous year’s total, according to the bureau records reviewed in a New York Times investigation. Reporters found that some later appeared at auctions associated with slaughter buyers. Bureau of Land Management events in 2026 advertised sale-eligible horses for as little as $25 . A low price does not prove bad intent. It does make a fast resale more profitable. Pair that bargain price with no post-sale tracking, and the federal protection system begins to look suspiciously like an honor system.

The paperwork sounds formidable. Buyers must promise humane care and certify that they will not knowingly transfer an animal to anyone intending to send it to slaughter or process it into commercial products. A knowingly false statement to the federal government may violate U.S.C. § 1001 , which generally carries a maximum prison term of five years. But a sternly worded form cannot follow a horse to its auction. Someone has to check.

The Bureau of Land Management has responded with stronger safeguards , yet they are small steps toward a resolution. Its updated policy sets a standard $125 price, generally limits buyers to four animals every six months, strengthens the bill of sale and allows officials to bar purchasers linked to kill pens or commercial processing . While those are sensible changes, they’re not enough. A horse can fetch up to $750 or more for illicit resale at a slaughter plant. A disturbingly lucrative flipping operation at the expense of a life. Most important, the Bureau of Land Management has yet to mandate post-sale oversight.

In September, a bipartisan group of 18 lawmakers requested that the Government Accountability Office review the Bureau of Land Management’s Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program. Initiated by the co-chairs of the Congressional Wild Horse Caucus and Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), the Sept. 10 letter calls for an independent examination of purchaser screenings and post-sale oversight and enforcement. This includes whether the agency can identify repeat violators and recover animals that enter the slaughter pipeline. Congress has taken an important first step. Now it must follow through, using findings to close gaps in oversight and ensure its promise of protection survives the sale.

Ranchers, environmentalists and wild-horse advocates have legitimate disagreements about herd size, rangeland health, and humane population control. Those arguments deserve an honest debate, without loopholes undermining them. It’s time for Congress to demand accountability and transparency for the livelihood of America’s wild horses.

Manda Kalimian is the founder and president of Rewilding America Now, a nonprofit that advocates for conservation-based approaches to managing America’s wild horses.
